speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR PRESENT AND FUTURE PAYMENT OF ANNUITIES AND OTHER AMENDMENTS   CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
Neither have I any particular objection to the amendment moved to the bill by Their Honours in the other place, but it does seem to me to be somewhat unnecessary, especially in view of the clearly established control of the House of Commons and the Senate over their employees. Further I should like to point out that the concern which would seem to have prompted this amendment relates to only one point. The subsection of the section in the Public Service Superannuation Act which the Senate wishes to amend is the subsection giving the governor in council power to pass regulations to determine an age beyond which contributors to the public service superannuation fund shall not be continued in employment.
Of course that section applies only to contributors. It does not apply to other employees, of whom we have many in both the House of Commons and the Senate. Even with respect to those to whom the section can apply, it means that the only concern expressed in the Senate amendment is the concern over our right in the House of Commons and the right of the Senate to keep people in our employment after they have passed a certain age.
It seems to me that there are other matters affecting our employees which should give us much greater concern than that. In fact, the only reason I can see for our wanting the right to continue certain employees after a certain age is because we have no pension for them. In other words the aim of this amendment is to keep ourselves in the position of being able to say to some of the employees who have served us faithfully for many years, "We are sorry, we have no pension for you, but we will give you the privilege of continuing to work for us as long as you can walk in the door." That is not good enough.
As I said, I have no particular objection to the amendment; but I think the other place and this House of Commons should be concerned about something more than the one point with which it deals. We should be concerned about finding some way of establishing a proper pension plan for those who have served both the Senate and the House of Commons across the years, including those who serve us for many years on a sessional basis.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the discussion on section 1 of this bill I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the fact that this bill is merely extending the practice of confining in local jails prisoners who are serving sentences of less than two years. I do not know what the situation is in the rest of Canada, but I do know that the situation in regard to that particular matter in the area from which I come is very bad indeed.
For example, within the last few weeks I have seen newspaper clippings

no doubt the minister has seen them also-indicating that in the county jail in that area where most of the prisoners are confined there is a long waiting list. The prison there was built some 50 years ago when the population was perhaps only 50 per cent of what it is today. It was built to accommodate some 45 prisoners. From the latest press stories I have seen, 75 persons are now confined in that institution.
There is no sleeping accommodation; they are doubling up in the cells, and sleeping on tables. I saw an item a few days ago in the press indicating that 50 people who were to be confined in that institution could not be accepted because there was not room for them.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO CONTINUE PROVISION RESPECTING CUSTODY OF NEWFOUNDLAND PRISONERS
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt
my hon. friend, but I must point out to him
Criminal Code
that the condition of which he speaks has nothing to do with the bill now before us. The general practice in all the provinces of Canada, with the exception of Newfoundland, is for those who have been sentenced to terms of imprisonment of less than two years to be sent to provincial jails of the type he has described in his own province.
We have no control over any jails. They are under the control of the provincial authorities, and if there is inadequate accommodation in his district I suggest it is a matter for the provincial authorities.
The purpose of this bill is to introduce what is a quite exceptional arrangement, and one which does not prevail in any of the other provinces in Canada. Its purpose is to authorize an institution in Newfoundland which is used as a provincial jail to be also used as a federal penitentiary. The reason for this arrangement is that in Newfoundland the percentage of the population which have become lawbreakers is so very much smaller than the average figure in Canada. Only 29 persons are serving sentences of two years and over, as penitentiary inmates, in this institution in Newfoundland. Obviously the setting up of all the paraphernalia and machinery of a penitentiary for that number of inmates would be unwarranted.
We suggested earlier that we might remove these Newfoundland convicts from Newfoundland to Dorchester penitentiary in New Brunswick; but both the Newfoundland authorities and the Newfoundland prisoners themselves did not wish to have this done. The prisoners preferred to stay in the Newfoundland institution. We think the arrangements made for their accommodation in Newfoundland, on the whole, are quite good. The arrangement is working out very well; it is very economical, and it is satisfactory for all concerned. These are the reasons we ask for the approval of this bill.
The subject matter of the bill has nothing to do with the condition in his province about which my hon. friend from Cape Breton South speaks. If there is inadequate accommodation there, it is a matter which should be taken up by him with the provincial authorities.

-this is no time to discuss the merits or demerits of the old age pension laws of Canada. I have had no opportunity to confer with my colleagues about this motion. Therefore anything I say today must be taken as being said entirely on my own responsibility and as giving my own views. I think all hon. members will agree that it would be unfair for me to attempt to commit any of my colleagues when there has been no opportunity for previous consideration.
I would point out that the amendment merely asks that consideration be given. It reads as follows:
"this house is of the opinion that consideration should be given to increasing the payments made to our old age and blind pensioners, under the Old Age Assistance Act, the Old Age Security Act and the Blind Persons Act, to an amount commensurate with today's cost of living."
It does not call for an increase to any specific amount. In fact, it gives no details whatever, but merely asks that consideration should be given to this question of an increase for these Canadians who are living under such great handicaps. I intend to support the amendment because I believe that a message should go forward from this parliament to the new parliament of Canada indicating that we believe this whole question should be thoroughly reviewed by that new parliament. Such action cannot be taken this Monday morning or this week. The question would have to be carefully investigated, probably by a committee such as that which some years ago dealt with the old age security problem and the problem of our blinded Canadians.
I am convinced that these problems are of sufficient importance to warrant such a careful investigation by the new parliament. In the hope that what we are doing today will emphasize to the members of the new parliament the need for another look at this problem and also that it will emphasize the unfortunate condition under which these Canadians are carrying on at the present time, I intend to support the amendment.

I am glad to hear him say
that he was speaking for himself because I would hate to think his party's policy is that we should let this stand over for consideration at another session.
The figures put on the record by the member for Winnipeg North Centre very clearly indicate that this question of where you get the money, increasing taxation and so forth in order to pay the bill, is a fallacy. Members of the house who have sat on committees during the last eight years, particularly on the old age security committee, will remember that top ranking economists, speaking of the ability to pay, talked about our gross national product being $11 billion at that time. From that figure of $11 billion they figured what the country could afford to pay in old age security then. Our argument has always been that the economy of the country is not static. It is a big country and the greater the redistribution of wealth the greater the ability of people in the country to buy. Many people speaking in the house have said that we have got to find markets and that we should have greater internal consuming markets. This would be one way to get them.
The figures put on the record by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre indicate that there has been a terrific increase in the gross national product-an increase of approximately $8 billion-since there has been any increase in old age pensions and blind pensions. A lot of other people in the country have benefited and their standards of living have gone up. There are many people who have more than they need. The amendment by the member for Winnipeg North Centre would mean that you would be placing more purchasing power in the hands of people in this country who are getting very little on the income they have at the present time. If an increase were given all of that money would go for the purchase of
Old Age and Blind Pensions food, clothing and shelter-although it would not provide nearly enough of that. The purchasing power of a large number of citizens would be increased. They would buy the products of industry and in so doing would stimulate production in the country and everyone would benefit as a result. Payment of old age security pensions provides for redistribution of wealth and I think that the government would be well advised to consider this amendment at the present time.
The amendment only says that the government should give consideration to this matter. It does not ask the government to adopt the suggestion and then run out and put it into operation immediately. I would suggest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that he should say that the government is considering this and is prepared to accept the amendment because that is what the government is doing all the time anyway. The amendment takes in blind pensioners and old age security pensioners and poses a straight question to the government. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, we are dealing here with one problem, not a double-barrelled problem; and I think it is a reasonable request.

Mr. Chairman, when the house rose at ten o'clock on Saturday I was making some introductory remarks with regard to two matters. I was supporting the suggestion that a standing committee on veterans affairs be set up and I suggested also that that standing committee might properly review the work of the Canadian pension commission to see whether or not the interpretation of the Pension Act by that commission was in accordance with the will and purpose of parliament when the act was drafted and to discover whether or not assistance would be given to the commission if suitable amendments to the act were passed.
As an illustration of these matters I was drawing attention to the case of Corporal MacAulay who was killed while in charge of a military vehicle in Winnipeg in 1950.
I shall endeavour to make my remarks as brief as possible, but I want to set out this case clearly because if it serves as a model for future decisions, if the commissioners are adopting the principle of stare decisis, then I think it is necessary to take a second look at the act. Further, if this case is allowed to stand as it is I think some further information should be obtained by the Department


of Veterans Affairs from the Department of National Defence as to certain aspects of military service.
I want to make it clear at the start that this particular case has received that type of complete and detailed examination that we have learned to expect from the Canadian pension commission. The case came before the commissioners in the first instance on September 1, 1950. It came before the commissioners again on April 26, 1951. An appeal board held a hearing on this case on March 6, 1952. On March 2, 1953, an appeal board heard argument concerning leave to reopen. I am informed that if the matter is pressed sympathetic consideration will be given to an application for another hearing on the question of leave to reopen. I am hesitating at the moment whether that course should be followed. I appeared at the appeal board hearing on March 2, 1953, and I am not sure whether their finding against leave to reopen was due to my representations or in spite of them. However, the point is that the Canadian pension commission does give most careful consideration to these cases and I commend them for that practice.
I wish to draw attention to the findings of the appeal board of March 6, 1952. I shall read them so that they are clearly on the record, and I quote:
As a result of its careful and sympathetic examination of the circumstances the board is unable to find that the condition causing death is pensionable under the provisions of section 11-2. It did not "arise out of service", there being no compulsion on the part of the deceased to use the jeep. While authority was granted to him to use the vehicle, this was not a military order. Neither can the board find that the cause of death was "directly connected with military service" as it has not been shown that the use of a military vehicle by the deceased was a "requirement" of service in any way.
The application therefore cannot be granted.
And on March 2, 1953, the appeal board which was considering whether or not leave to reopen should be granted, made the following finding:
The board carefully reviewed all available evidence and was unable to establish that:
(1)	Any degree of compulsion attended the act of Corporal MacAulay borrowing the service jeep for his personal use;
(2)	The interests of the service were in any way involved by this act.
The board concludes that no useful purpose would be served by allowing leave to reopen this case as the issues involved do not appear to come within the provisions of section 11 (2) of the Pension Act.
Mr. Chairman, there are three portions of the Pension Act to which I wish to draw attention. The commission is empowered to interpret the act. That provision is found in section 5, subsection 3, which reads as follows:

The commission shall determine any question of interpretation of this act and the decision of the commission on any such question shall be final.
The other section-and this is the one that, as I said on Saturday, causes all the trouble -is section 11, subsection 2, of which I will read just the concluding three and a half lines:
. . . when the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death in respect of which the application for pension is made arose out of or was directly connected with such military service.
The third section with which I should like to deal later on is section 63, the "benefit of doubt" section. Section 11, subsection 2, dealing with what constitutes military service or with the expression "arising out of military service" is, as I said, the one section of the act which seems to cause the greatest difficulty. In this particular case that I am using as an example-and there are others, of course, that I could give-they found, as I have read, that Corporal MacAulay was considered not to be engaged in military service.
My concluding remarks on Saturday had to do with the use, in the findings of the appeal board, of that expression "borrowing" a military vehicle. I expressed surprise that that word should have been used. I thought that the word "borrow" was not part of the army vocabulary.
Just briefly the facts of this particular case are as follows. The sergeant who was in charge of military vehicles at Fort Osborne barracks in the year 1950-whom I shall call Sergeant X-walked from the sergeants' mess to the vehicle park, got the jeep, brought it over to the sergeants' mess and handed it over to Corporal MacAulay. The evidence brought out in the military courts of inquiry, of which there were two, indicated that Sergeant X had handed over the vehicle to Corporal MacAulay. In other words, he had placed Corporal MacAulay in charge of the military vehicle.
It seems to me to be a little bit irrelevant to discuss what was the nature of the mission on which Corporal MacAulay subsequently went, although I may deal with that matter later. But it is on that point where my military experience differs so widely from the finding of the appeal board and I wonder then about this question of interpretation of the act. I was always under the impression that if a person was placed in charge of a military vehicle, the responsibility for that placing rested on higher authority and that the person who was driving the vehicle was on military duty. He obviously must be in charge of military equipment while he is using that
Supply-Veterans Affairs vehicle. If he is using the vehicle for some purpose that is not normal, I would not consider that the responsibility would be upon the user of the vehicle but rather on higher authority. The commission seems to consider that something in the nature of borrowing vehicles for private and personal use was in operation at Fort Osborne barracks at that particular time and, that being the case, that the user of the borrowed vehicle assumed the entire responsibility.
It occurred to me that that situation indicated that there was, if not a breakdown in military discipline at Fort Osborne barracks, perhaps a lapse on that particular occasion and that the responsibility rested on Sergeant X, the unknown officer in charge of vehicles, and on the commander of the units or the area.
How are we to determine what constitutes service unless there is something in the Interpretation Act which gives guidance to the commission? The commissioners take a view which, to my mind, is diametrically opposed to the experience of people who have served in the forces. I will just summarize the clarification that is needed in this connection. For the guidance of the commissioners and in the general interests of all those who are serving in the forces, I think the Department of Veterans Affairs should ask the Department of National Defence to assist by giving answers to questions such as the following:
1.	May army vehicles be borrowed? If so, are the users of borrowed vehicles informed that in the event of injury they have no claim for pension and that in the event of death their dependents have no claim?
2.	May army vehicles be dispatched on trips without a vehicle work ticket signed by proper authority? If so, are the drivers of vehicles thus dispatched aware of the fact that in the event of injury or death no claim for pension will be granted?
3.	If an officer or non-commissioned officer places a person junior to him in rank in charge of an army vehicle, is the person thus placed acting with authority or without authority? If he is acting with authority, on whom does the responsibility lie in case of injury or fatal accident?
In other words, is it possible for a member of the army to be in charge of an army vehicle without being on duty? The case of Corporal MacAulay seems to me to raise this particular issue which requires clarification. ' If the interpretation followed by the commissioners in this matter of military service permits the shifting of responsibilities from the high command in the army down

Supply-Veterans Affairs to a private soldier or a junior N.C.O., I think there is perhaps a misconception of military discipline there.
Another point arises in this connection. In one instance the commission said that this was not a military order, and, in the other finding, they say there was no compulsion on the corporal to use the vehicle. In the hearing of arguments I recall the suggestion of one of the commissioners to me that an N.C.O. should resist what he considers to be or what might be considered to be an improper order. Well, if that is the case I think our people serving in the forces will have to be informed, because I have never known the army to be a debating society. I do not think you can have people suggesting to senior officers that what they are instructed to do should not be done. My experience is that you carry out orders and, if you feel like it, you protest about them afterwards. You cannot carry on debate in the army. Our democracy cannot afford more than one debating chamber. Somebody has to carry on the work of the country while others talk about it as I am doing at the moment.
How can the pension commissioners, with a background of military service, suggest that there is no compulsion when a vehicle is handed over by a senior N.C.O. to a junior N.C.O.? How could the corporal say to the sergeant, "No, sergeant, I do not want the vehicle. You should not be giving it to me under these circumstances." I fail to understand how they can say that.
I just want to deal for a moment with the benefit of doubt clause and sum up what I think has been the result of the commission's findings. The benefit of doubt clause, which is No. 63, reads as follows:
Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
I have always been of the opinion that the clause was introduced into the act in order to assist the commissioners in cases where decisions are extremely difficult. I thought it was introduced into the act so that there would be no difficulty about relieving hardship; and that a certain freedom of action would be permitted to allow the commissioners to go a little beyond the specified sections elsewhere in the act in order to look after those who were suffering in one way or another from disability-or to look after those dependents who were placed in difficult circumstances. It occurred

to me that after all evidence had been heard in a case where the finding of the commission might reasonably, on legal grounds, be considered to be against the applicant, then attention would be paid to section 63, the matter weighed again, and a decision given on the side of generosity. I thought that was the purpose of the particular section in the act and that it was the general idea held by members of the House of Commons about the section when it was drafted. I may be quite wrong in all of this and I am prepared to have my errors pointed out, but again let me use my case of Corporal MacAulay to indicate a situation where in my opinion benefit of doubt did occur.
The evidence of the two courts seemed to indicate that Corporal MacAulay obtained the vehicle from Sergeant X in order to perform or go on some mission of his-to visit his home and pick up some of his supplies. I do not wish to implicate the sergeant, whom I do not know, and I do not wish to cast aspersions on any sergeant in the Canadian army; for sergeants are the backbone of the army. However, I suggest that an element of doubt arises when you consider the facts that were brought out in the courts of inquiry. For one thing, the sergeant in charge of the vehicles went and got the vehicle himself. No sergeant ever did that for me when I was a corporal. The sergeant did not make out a work ticket to authorize the trip and thereby infringed upon army regulations. The sergeant asked the corporal into the sergeants' mess, infringing upon the regulations in so doing, and primed him with drinks. Finally, the sergeant waited up until a late hour of the night for the corporal to return. Well, I suggest there is some slight element of doubt that the trip which Corporal MacAulay made was solely for his own purposes. I may be quite wrong but I thought there was a loophole for some doubt in the matter.
I now wish to sum up what I have been saying and I think that the MacAulay case emphasizes the following points:
1.	That in the opinion of 50 per cent of the panel of commissioners-because certainly six of the twelve commissioners have reviewed the evidence in this-there has been a practice if not widespread in the army certainly operative on at least one occasion at Fort Osborne barracks, Winnipeg, of what the commissioners call "borrowing" of vehicles and that under these circumstances the "borrower" assumes full responsibility.
2.	That the commissioners do not recognize in the use of army vehicles without vehicle work tickets a lapse or breakdown in army discipline and a consequent responsibility on

the higher command rather than on the user of the vehicle.
3.	That the commissioners are of the opinion that a junior N.C.O. may and should resist carrying out the orders or instructions of a senior N.C.O. if that order or instruction appears not to be strictly in the interests of the service or, to use the words of the commissioners, if there is no "compulsion" involved.
4.	That the commissioners do not consider that the benefit of doubt clause should be invoked in favour of the applicant when the entire evidence against the applicant is given by only one person.
In explanation of the last point I would say that the applicant was the widow. The only available evidence was that of the sergeant. Corporal MacAulay was not living and could give no explanation about why he had the vehicle or where he had gone. Again I thought that an element of doubt might have been invoked there.
I raise this problem, Mr. Chairman, because I think there is an increasing number of injuries and fatal accidents occurring within the armed services at the present time. The number of such incidents has vastly increased. With highway traffic accidents mounting there is a constant problem facing the commission with regard to men who are injured or killed while they are on leave or absent from their stations. Cases of that kind are brought to my attention and it is difficult for the average person to understand why a man who is in the service of his country and who suffers an injury while on leave or away from his station should not be able to receive a pension on that account. It is even more difficult, in the case of a fatal accident, for the dependents to understand why they cannot be given greater consideration than they receive now in the way of pension. We are asking men to enter the services. Within the services now I think we have about 40 per cent in the married category. The dependents of these men are being placed in a difficult position in the case of fatal accidents. Surely some clarification is necessary in so far as these people are concerned. I think the commission would welcome attention to this matter by the House of Commons, and perhaps some clarification of the interpretation section of the act or some modification or some of these sections that would make the work of the commission somewhat easier.
I do not doubt for one minute that, in the words of the commission, they give very sympathetic consideration to every case that comes before them. I have confidence in the
Supply-Veterans Affairs pension commission. I think the commission is hampered and their work is curtailed by the wording of the act itself or the fact that the act needs some extension. Consequently, my suggestion in regard to this matter is that, either through a standing committee on veterans affairs, as has been suggested, or in some other way, the work of the pension commission should be reviewed to ascertain the type of cases being presented; the number of dismissals and the reasons therefor; the interpretation placed by the commissioners on section 11, subsection 2; the use and effectiveness of section 63, the benefit of doubt section; and finally what clarification or amendment of the act may be required to fulfil the purposes of'parliament.

I do not feel that I should allow this item to pass during the dying days of this parliament without having at least a few words to say in connection with the veterans. I want to express to the minister my appreciation of the steps he has taken during his term of office towards following up the good work started by his predecessors the Right Hon. Ian Mackenzie and the present Minister of Labour, Hon. Mr. Gregg. I should not allow this occasion to pass without expressing my sincere appreciation of the good work done by the parliamentary assistant, the hon. member for Winnipeg South. He has done a wonderful job in the committee, and when any of us have referred questions to him he has not allowed any grass to grow under his feet until he has done everything within the confines of the legislation to get the matter straightened out. While he has told us that this is his last session of parliament, I hope that in whatever work he undertakes-I hope that will be in connection with veterans-he will be successful and will have many happy days of useful work ahead.
Having said that, I am going to say something now which I hope the minister and his assistant will take to heart. I hope they will complete the work they have carried on thus far. I am referring in particular to the war veterans' allowance that has been under discussion for a number of years. Last year the allowance was increased from $40 for single men and $70 for married veterans to $50 for single and $90 for married veterans.
The veterans organizations across the country have requested that these allowances be increased to $60 per month for the single veteran and $120 for the married veteran. I do not feel that this is asking too much at the present time. Even though we are burdened with a Liberal government, we are living in the best country in the world.

Supply-Veterans Affairs It would not have been possible for our national production to reach $23 billion in 1952 were it not for the services rendered by the veterans for whom we are now asking this increase in veterans' allowances. The resources of the country today will allow for this increase to be given. We should like very much to have this increase that has been requested by veterans organizations all across the country granted.
During the past few weeks I have received letters from the Legion branches at Edger-ton, Irma, Viking and Camrose and other points that I cannot recall at the moment. I should like to have the minister, his assistant and their cabinet colleagues look into this matter' and take care of it before this session finishes. The ceilings on earnings now are $720 for single men and $1,200 for married men. These ceilings do not seem to be in line with present conditions. Again I would urge that these ceilings be increased from the present level to $1,200 for single men and $2,000 for married men. In case the government cannot see its way clear to doing that, I think there should be an increase to at least the income tax ceilings of $1,000 for single men and $2,000 for married men. I feel that the means test should be removed altogether when these veterans reach the age of 60. For many years it has been recognized these veterans are pre-aged by 10 years. If the means test were eliminated at 60, this would put them on the same footing as the civilians who reach the age of 70 and receive a pension of $40 per month without any means test. I hope that before this session finishes something will be done to implement these requests.
The question of a permanent committee on veterans affairs has been mentioned. I hope that that will be taken care of also before this session ends. We have had a piling up of troublesome cases, as well as the need of a possible revision of the legislation dealing with the veterans charter. If we had had a permanent veterans affairs committee, these irritations would not have been allowed to continue to cause dissatisfaction throughout the country. I am not going into detail on these matters because the hon. member for Acadia, who has rendered a very useful service over the years since he came into this house, touched upon many matters.
There is one last group I want to mention. Just as soon as possible I should like to see the remaining few soldier settlers, about 500, given clear title to their land. Many of them have been working on these farms trying to pay for them since 1919 when the legislation was passed. I should like to see the minister complete a fairly good job by having these


matters to which I have referred taken care of before this session is concluded.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.
The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I am not going to take up very much of the time of the committee. My province and my constituency take a great deal of interest in this department of government affairs. During world wars I and II my province had the record and the honour of having more enlistments per capita than any other province of Canada.
I am not a war veteran myself, and therefore I know the committee will pardon me for saying a few words at this time. However, I am the son of a war veteran who had a distinguished career in the civil war between the states in 1864. Because of the treatment my father received at the hands of the United States government some 25 or 30 years after that war ended I became a great believer in pensions. At that time soldiers received very small pay when compared with what they receive today. I want to put this on the record. When my father finally caught up with his pension he was paid $8 a month, which was the full wage of a private at that time, from the date of his discharge, plus 3 per cent compound interest, to the time he got his pension some 20 years afterwards. They continued that, and finally at the time of his death in 1899 he was receiving the princely sum of $50 a month, which was a big pension when you compare the value of the dollar in those days with the value today. Furthermore, my mother drew the same pension for some 36 years after my father's death. The United States was the first country in the world to pay a soldier a pension and let him live under any flag he liked and spend his money as he wished.
As I said a moment ago, I am not a war veteran. I have been connected with political matters for a long time, and because of that I have been closely connected with pensions, veterans' allowances and so on for the last 25 years.
I wish to say that in taking up pension matters with the department here in Ottawa on behalf of the veterans of my constituency, beginning with the men at the bottom rung of the ladder who have to do with pensioners and soldiers' difficulties, right up to the highest officers in the pension commission, I have had the best of service and every courtesy shown to me in my appeals on behalf of those veterans. I think I can safely say that 99 per cent of the men who have to do with taking care of pensions and dealing with

soldiers have been and are doing an excellent job.
I had always hoped that a veterans committee would be set up during the present session similar to the one that was set up a few years ago. When that is done one who is not a veteran can always take his troubles to the veterans committee, and when he does not understand the matters with which he is dealing, he can get the best advice from the war veterans committee. I do hope that soon we shall have a veterans committee in this House of Commons that will give the same service as-or probably better service than-the last veterans committee gave.	.
I have had considerable difficulty with respect to getting widows' pensions. One of the objections arises in connection with certificates of death. I have had several of that kind. I mention it in the committee today because it is hard to understand that there should be this difference of opinion among medical authorities. I have had a great deal of trouble with regard to certain definitions such as employable and unemployable, amnesia, army alcoholic, and a few others. It is sometimes difficult to find out what the department means by an unemployable veteran and an employable one. There does not seem to be any definition laid down that is workable in these cases. That is also true of amnesia.
The minister will remember that I had a case of amnesia up before him, and we had a good deal of trouble over it. Today, thanks to the department and the officials, we have that matter properly taken care of-at least I think so, and the department must also be of the same opinion.
Another point of interest to the department is the definition of an alcoholic or, as it is described in letters I have received, an army alcoholic. I have before me several cases in which this term is involved. At first they have always been turned down. I sought from different people information as to why a man would be classified as an alcoholic, and I believe the most convincing definition I received was from one of the applicants on whose behalf I was working. This is the way he, a private, defined an army alcoholic: A private who can consume more liquor than his commanding officer.
I must say that this definition must have been given favourable consideration by the pension board, because this man is now receiving a pension, and is now in the position of drawing down a good salary in the work he is now doing, for which he is well qualified. Notwithstanding that, he was first classified as an alcoholic, and could not be dealt with.
Supply-Veterans Affairs
During the last three or four weeks I have recommended to different government departments certain veterans for positions. These veterans were all from my own constituency, of course, and were well qualified for the positions they were seeking. Not one of them however was given priority in the filling of positions; not one was given advantage of the veterans preference. I am sure if the committee on veterans affairs were sitting it would look into these matters very carefully.
About a month ago I had brought to my attention the case of a man drawing a war veteran's allowance of about $80. He did not have and could not get a job. This amount was not quite sufficient for the needs of his family, with the result that his wife began to work part time. She was employed as waitress in a hotel and as she was performing her duties with efficiency, her services soon were in demand, with the result that she was making a reasonably good wage. As the result of investigations, however, the veteran had to take a reduction in the amount of his veteran's allowance, and he has been instructed to pay back the excess he has received while she has been working.
I believe it was the hon. member for Royal who said the other day that this is a ridiculous state of affairs and that it should not apply to any veteran who has seen service outside of Canada, or even to one who had not gone overseas but had served in the army. Surely a man in this position should be permitted to earn what he can in addition to his veteran's allowance, and the same should apply to any member of his family, without any deduction being made in the allowance he has received formerly.
I had some further comments to make, but I shall not take the time to do so now. I would point out that in my constituency, in common with many others, many veterans are to be found. As the years go by the demand for their services becomes less. In view of the fact that there are not many of these men in Canada now I suggest they should be given every consideration. When the law and regulations are so strict I suggest the officials at the top should be permitted to exercise discretion and, even if in all cases the strict letter of the law is not complied with, these men should have sympathetic consideration. They are real veterans who have done their part in a time of war.
I recall the first claim I ever made on behalf of a pensioner in my constituency. It was about 23 or 24 years ago that I brought this first case to Ottawa and placed it before the chief advocates and, following that, placed it before the pension board. The application was made on behalf of the widow, and

Supply-Veterans Affairs I found that the file contained reams of documents, including hundreds of letters written by politicians, clergymen, relatives and friends, all favouring the giving of the pension to the widow.
The difficulty was that on August 5, 1914, the young man in question had put on a soldier's uniform and had started off to Canso to perform his military duties. He died on August 6, having worn the uniform only one day. I am glad to say after considerable difficulty the pension was given to the widow.
Let me repeat, Mr. Chairman, that the officers in the different departments with which I have had to do business, from the very lowest to the highest, have always given me every consideration, and I take this opportunity to express my thanks to them, one and all. May I thank the committee for allowing me an opportunity to speak at this time, although I am not a veteran.

Mr. Chairman, I shall not take more than a moment in this discussion. I, too, would like to pay a compliment to the staff and personnel administering the Pension Act. I think that so far as British Columbia is concerned they have received co-operation, and particularly from the Legion.
While we are referring to the department, and its paternal interest in veterans affairs in general, may I say that I feel sometimes there is too great a stress laid upon the paternal angle in that they are apt to treat returned men as youngsters, children, or people to be cared for, and they are not left with that degree of freedom to which they are entitled.
I refer to those in receipt of war veterans' allowances who are not permitted to earn more than a certain sum of money. The amount they are allowed to earn is so small that, in view of the high cost of living today -and this is particularly true in my province -these people are not living at a very high standard. I have a letter from one veteran who helped to supplement his pension by raising chickens. The other day he wrote to me saying that the chicken operations had been so prolific that his income had risen to the point where it was above the limit, with the result that he had to sell his chickens, and that today he is doing nothing. I would ask the minister to reconsider his decision and remove the means test from this particular pension.
There is one other matter I should like to bring to the minister's attention. I have had one or two local cases which have been marginal in character where there has been some doubt as to whether the man had died as a result of service overseas. In one case the decision was quite doubtful; as a matter


of fact I still feel that it was wrong. The result is that the widow and two children are receiving no pension. I am satisfied and the doctors who knew this man are satisfied that he died as a result of service. There is in the act a section which is supposed to give the benefit of the doubt to a pensioner or to a pensioner's widow, but I am afraid that that section is not clear enough. I have come across many cases where the benefit of the doubt has not been given to the widow.
I urge the minister to issue instructions to all boards that in future greater consideration must be given to the power that they have to give the benefit of the doubt to a widow or to the orphaned children of a returned man. I ask the minister to listen to the plea of the returned men in general, particularly the Canadian Legion, in connection with the war veterans allowance and their request that it be increased to $60 per month for single and $120 for married men. In doing that I do believe he would be carrying out the wishes, not only of the returned men themselves but of the people of Canada who are anxious to pay their debt, who are willing to pay their debt and who are able to pay their debt to the men who defended them in time of need.

Mr. Chairman, this will be our last opportunity in this parliament to say a word on behalf of our old comrades. I should like to place before the committee my thoughts on four subjects having to do with veterans' affairs but before doing so I wish to express a word of admiration for the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, the hon. member for Winnipeg South, who is retiring from public life at the end of this session.
The hon. member came into the house with me in 1935, and since that time we have served together on every veterans affairs committee. We have always been on opposite sides when there has been disagreement in that committee, but we have become close friends from that association. I am only too glad to be able to say today that I think he has rendered a wonderful service on behalf of the veterans of Canada. Throughout these years he has been terribly in earnest about their problems. He has been very hard-working and conscientious, and in fact within the last year has given so much to this particular work that he has endangered his own health.
I understand that he may be appointed to the Canadian pension commission. Perhaps I should not say that, because I do not know, but I hope it will be the case. In the capacity of a commissioner he will be able to carry on with his work for his comrades

with whom he served in both the first and second world wars. I am sure I speak tor all hon. members who have served on veterans' committees when I wish him good luck and say that we shall be watching his work with great interest. We feel confident he will do it with great satisfaction to himself and benefit to the nation as a whole.
It is rather significant that of the 62 members who served on the veterans affairs committees in 1945 and 1946, when the so-called veterans' charter was considered, only half are now in the house. The rest of them have gone to different spheres of action. One never knows; perhaps half of the remaining half will be gone by this time next year, and that may include myself. Because this is the end of this parliament and because veterans' affairs have been my main interest throughout the past 18 years, I should like to place before the committee with all the emphasis at my command my views on four different subjects.
The first is the Pension Act. This act is the arch upon which all veterans' legislation has been built. It is the key to the veterans' charter. The keystone of that arch is the action known as the benefit of the doubt clause. This is section 63, which reads:
63. Notwithstanding anything in this act, on any application for pension, the applicant shall be entitled to the benefit of the doubt, which shall mean that it shall not be necessary for him to adduce conclusive proof of his right to the pension applied for, but the body adjudicating on the claim shall draw from all the circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced and medical opinions, all reasonable inferences and presumptions in favour of the applicant.
That benefit of the doubt clause was placed in the Pension Act many years ago and expresses clearly the intent of all parliaments of Canada since the first world war. I believe that by and large the officials of the Department of Veterans Affairs have endeavoured throughout the years to keep that clause in mind. But it is something which must be drawn repeatedly to their attention, to the attention of members of the house, and to the attention of the people of Canada. I suggest to the minister that it would be well worth while for him to have that section printed under the heading "benefit of the doubt" and placed on the desk of every official of the Department of Veterans Affairs from coast to coast, as well as on his own. If that were done it would be a great help to his officials in remembering that the people of Canada through their parliament have expressed the determination that the benefit of the doubt should be given to the veteran. That applies not only to the Pension Act but to all the other acts contained in the veterans' charter. The intent
Supply-Veterans Affairs behind all those acts has been that where any reasonable doubt exists, that doubt should be given to the veteran.
My second point has to do with the war veterans' allowance. In the special committee which sat last year we considered the war veterans' allowance. A revised act was recommended to the house and placed on the statute books of Canada. However, there was serious disagreement in the committee about two features of that revised War Veterans Allowance Act. One was the amount of the allowance which by the act was placed at $50 for a single veteran and $90 for a married man. The Canadian Legion and the national council-those two great organizations of the veterans of Canada-asked that the figures be $60 for the single veteran and $120 for the married one. Some of us in the committee did our best to bring about an increase to those figures.
Under our present provisions there is what is known as a war veterans assistance fund from which a single veteran can get help up to $10 a month or a married veteran can get up to a maximum of $15 a month, after passing a second means test. There is this provision for a handout in certain cases; but we believe that help could very well be included in the allowance itself and that these veterans, who after all are front-line veterans -they cannot qualify at all if they have not served in a theatre of war, except in the case of a few who are small pensioners-should be given that $60 a month if single and $120 a month if married.
In recent years there has been too much tendency to get the veteran into the same position as that of the civilian in so far as welfare is concerned. The Legion dealt with that matter in the Legionary in December of last year when they used this sentence in reporting on the brief which had been submitted in that month to the cabinet:
There is no serious argument that the present basic rates are adequate to meet the needs of the veteran entirely dependent on W.V.A., but we have been told that the insuperable objection to granting our request is that W.V.A. legislation must be tied to the provisions of the Old Age Pensions Act. We are not prepared to accept that proposition.
The other departments of government must not be allowed to interfere in this veterans legislation. The veteran served Canada; he is the responsibility of Canada; he should be treated on his own merits and should not be tied in with whatever welfare legislation there may be.
Then there was a second ground of dispute in the committee last year with respect to war veterans allowance, and that was over the amount of permissive income which a veteran could receive without interfering with

Supply-Veterans Affairs his war veteran's allowance. At present he is allowed only $10 a month over his allowance, whether single or married, so that the total permissive income for a single veteran, including allowance, is $60 per month or a total of $720 per year and $100 a month or $1,200 a year if he is married. The veterans organizations asked that those figures he made $1,200 and $2,000 respectively. Before the revision of the act last year the single veteran had permissive income over his allowance of $125 a year, which is $5 more than he has now, and the married veteran had a permissive income of $250, which is $130 more than he now has. It is significant that under the Old Age Assistance Act the civilian recipients between the ages of 65 and 69 have a permissive income over the allowance of $20 a month or a total of $240 a year, whether they are single or married.
In the committee we tried hard to have that ceiling raised. Although the government members of the committee would not agree to a motion increasing the amount of the allowance itself, they did agree to a recommendation about this permissive income; and with regard to this permissive income, the committee brought into the house a year ago a unanimous finding, reading as follows:
Your committee further recommends to the government continued and sympathetic study of the needs and requirements of recipients of war veterans allowance, keeping in mind the recommendations of veterans organizations in that respect, and particularly with regard to permissive income.
As a result of that unanimous recommendation a year ago, I think we had reason to expect that during the present session the permissive income would be raised, but unfortunately that action has not been taken and it remains just as it was enacted in the bill a year ago.
Mr. Chairman, this ceiling on permissive income has extremely dire effects in many cases. For example, I have here a letter from a widow whose husband served with the first contingent. He went overseas with the first battalion from my home province of British Columbia. He had a distinguished career overseas. These people lost their only child in the air force in the second war. The husband finally reached a financial position where he was obliged to take the war veterans' allowance. Now he also has passed on. The widow finds herself caught by this ceiling. She cannot get the war veteran's allowance which goes to a widow plus the old age pension because the ceiling enters into the picture. She is allowed the $40 old age security pension but then she is allowed only $20 war veterans' allowance instead of the $50 which she would otherwise have received.


That is the situation because there is the ceiling of $60 a month in her case. Here is what she says:
I think we are the only ones that don't benefit at all from the Old Age Pensions Act which seems unfair. If I had both, i.e. $100 a month, I could continue to live in my small house in the country, but if I am to start having O.A.P. and only $20 from the veterans allowance, I shall have to sell it, as one cannot live on $60 a month, with taxes and everything up and paying my hospital insurance too, amongst other things.
That letter is tragically accurate in its facts. If the permissive income were raised to the extent that the recipient of old age security pension could also get the war veterans' allowance, it would make a tremendous difference in the lives of these Canadians.
Another example is that of the small pensioner. He did not get the full benefit from any increase in the war veterans' allowance or the increase in the pension because he is caught by the ceiling on permissive income. His pension went up but the war veterans' allowance came down. In my judgment these veterans have been unfairly treated because of the fact that the ceiling is kept so low.
A third example is the man or his wife who takes a small job. Their joint incomes are taken into consideration. If one or the other of them goes and takes a small job, the amount of the war veterans' allowance is reduced. This difficulty also would be overcome if the ceiling on permissive income were to be raised. If the new parliament does nothing else, I hope it will raise that ceiling in the first session.
One other point in connection with the war veterans' allowance is this fact which has been raised by several members already. The widow of an imperial veteran cannot qualify unless her husband lived in Canada for 20 years. Some of those men died after they had been here 18 or 19 years, but the widows cannot qualify even if they have been here for 30 years. The Legion dealt with that question last year in their recommendations to the cabinet. They asked:
That widows of allied ex-servicemen be granted the war veterans' allowance in cases where the husband died before completing 20 years' residence in Canada, provided that the widow herself has 20 years' residence and her husband was otherwise eligible.
Such a provision would be eminently fair. I think it is the only way in which we can interpret the wishes of the house.
The .third point about which I should like to make a suggestion has to do with the benevolent funds of the three forces and, particularly, the eligibility of those young Canadians who have been serving in our army

in Korea. Questions have been raised in the house. I questioned the Associate Minister of National Defence; and other members, the member for Brandon, for instance, have asked questions. There has been considerable confusion about this situation but I believe the position today is that while the veteran of the navy with Korean service, and the veteran of the air force with Korean service, have full access to the benevolent funds of those two great fighting forces, the veteran of the army with Korean service is not in that position. Why he should be put in an inferior position I cannot understand. It has been the army that has been suffering the casualties. I believe we have had far more army men in Korea than we have had men in the other forces. Those men should be put on exactly the same basis as the men who served in the navy and the air force.
The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, in answering a question last week, explained that there had been a welfare fund set up by the army but it did not give the same over-all coverage as that of the other two services. I may say that I do not blame him for saying this, and it does not detract from what I said about him a moment ago. He is simply speaking for the government, although I have a good idea of how he feels about the matter himself. Here is what he had to say at page 4839 of Hansard:
In the cases of veterans who require assistance but are not entitled to the Canadian army welfare fund assistance, the welfare officer does his best to obtain help through community resources, such as service clubs, Canadian Legion branches, army and navy branches, and such organizations as make it a practice to assist people in distress. A few of our district offices have at their disposal small trust funds, from which limited assistance can be provided.
That means, Mr. Chairman, that the veteran of army service in Korea has to go to a service club or to a Legion branch or to some other organization that helps people in distress in order to get the benefits that he should be getting from the army welfare fund. We do not require legislation to remedy this defect; it can be done by the government without the necessity of passing further laws-and I would hope that it would be done without any further delay.
Until a few weeks ago we had another rather anomalous situation with regard to army lads who had served in Korea in that they were not eligible for payment of clothing allowance or rehabilitation grant unless they had a total of 183 days' paid service outside North America. I believe that was changed about the middle of April, but before then a man who had served in Korea and had not
Supply-Veterans Affairs been there 183 days-even though he had been wounded in action, and. I had one such lad come to me about it-could not qualify for clothing allowance or rehabilitation grant. That situation should not have arisen at all.
The men who are serving in the army in Korea should certainly receive exactly the same consideration as men in the other forces. In my opinion nothing is too good for them.
Finally, may I say a word about the prisoner of war situation. As I understand the position, money from which any payments would come is German money. It is not money that has to be voted by the parliament of Canada -and even if it were I would not change my views on the point. If a Canadian was a prisoner of the Japanese or if he was a prisoner of any one of the group of organizations in Germany, such as the gestapo or the SS., he has been granted a payment of $1 per day for the time he was a captive.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If the hon. member is discussing benefits to prisoners of war I think he might more properly do that on the estimates of the Secretary of State.
No, Mr. Chairman, I have the right department here. The Department of Veterans Affairs is actually presenting cases for these men-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: No.

-before the war claims commission. It is being done by the veterans' bureau, and it is very much a problem of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The matter has been raised by other members and I submit that I am perfectly in order in discussing it today.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I recall that the hon. member for Royal referred to this question briefly but at that time it had not been drawn to my attention that, strictly speaking, the war claims commission actually comes under the Department of the Secretary of State. I really think discussion of this question would more properly take place when the estimates of the Secretary of State are before the committee.

Mr. Chairman, may I point out to you that the Minister of Veterans Affairs was the minister before whom the representations of the national council of Canadian prisoners of war were made this spring. It was the Minister of Veterans Affairs who heard those representations. They were rejected. It is true that the Secretary of State tabled a copy of a letter in which their requests were rejected, but within the last two or three weeks the Minister of Veterans Affairs has again heard representations from

Supply-Veterans Affairs this association. He is the minister whom the cabinet has. delegated to deal with this problem.
Further than that, as I pointed out, one branch of his department, the veterans' welfare bureau, is actually preparing claims for those prisoners of war and appears for them before the commission. I submit that I cannot be ruled out of order in discussing this matter. Actually, I only intend to take a very few minutes but for those reasons I do not believe that it would be right to rule me out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, personally, I have no objection if the hon. member wants to discuss this question on my estimates. I think your observations were quite proper, in that this matter does come under the Secretary of State. I should like to correct the hon. member when he says that I am responsible for this particular matter. I am not. It is true, as he pointed out, that I did receive the executive of the prisoner of war council, but I did so as a member of the cabinet and not particularly as Minister of Veterans Affairs. This fact was pointed out to them, and they understood it.
When the delegation returned a couple of weeks ago I was one of four or five ministers who saw them, but I did so as a cabinet minister and not as Minister of Veterans Affairs. However, it is quite true that we have made available to these people the services of the veterans bureau, just as we make the services of the department available in other cases. For instance, we do help certain veterans with their claims for unemployment insurance. I do not think that would give an hon. member the right to discuss unemployment insurance under the estimates of veterans affairs, simply because we render that service to some veterans. However, it is immaterial to me whether or not the matter is discussed.

I think I should be in the same position as representatives of this association, and should be allowed to place my statement before the Minister of Veterans Affairs. After all, he is the man who has to advise the cabinet on this question because the veterans of Canada are his responsibility.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Order. My only thought was to avoid a discussion of this subject on this item when, perhaps, it might be discussed more conveniently under the estimates of the Secretary of State. But in view of the fact the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra has pointed out, and the minister has confirmed, the fact that the veterans


bureau has taken part in this matter, perhaps the member for Vancouver-Quadra may be allowed to continue.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I am grateful to the minister for his help.
The other group of ex-prisoners of war which, of course, is by far the great majority, cannot get any assistance from the German reparations unless they establish a claim before the war claims commission. In order to establish that claim, they must prove, first of all, that they have been maltreated while prisoners of war. By the way, this is not easy for a young lad who was in a prisoner of war camp for three or four years. The men he knew there are now scattered all over the country. Many of them were not Canadians. From what I have been told by individual veterans, I know that it is a difficult thing to appear before that commission or send any representations to the commission, proving the actual maltreatment.
Not only must he prove maltreatment, but he must also prove that the maltreatment he suffered resulted in an incapacity to work, and that incapacity existed following his liberation. In other words, if he were beaten time after time while in a German prison camp, but when he was discharged could not prove that he had an incapacity to work at that time, he is not entitled to any claim on the reparations fund.
Now, there has been a nasty slur cast on the group in question, not from anyone in the government or from anyone on this side, but there have been suggestions that these soldiers surrendered and therefore do not deserve any consideration. It is suggested that if they get any consideration, then the whole Canadian army will surrender if it has to fight in another war. There have been nasty slurs of that kind going around the country. I need only point out to you, Mr. Chairman, to this house and to the Canadian people, two groups of these men who were prisoners.
In the first place, the Canadians who were captured at Dieppe form perhaps the largest group of army prisoners. These young men were thrown into the attack on Dieppe when there was not the slightest chance of their coming through. They were killed by hundreds. They were left on the beaches when the ships went away. What could they do but surrender? I do not believe there have ever been a more courageous group of young Canadians than those young men of Dieppe. Two of them won the V.C., but I do not doubt that there were dozens of others who deserved it.

1 have known of this sort of attack. My own battalion and three other battalions were put into a gas raid on Vimy Ridge on March 1, 1917, five or six weeks before the big attack. They were to go over and pick up the dead Germans who were supposed to have been killed by the gas sent over from our trenches. These men went over knowing they were facing certain death. The whole battalion knew it. Our colonel knew it. He was not supposed to go over. He was an Indian army veteran with a C.B. and a D.S.O., which he had won with our own 54th Kootenay battalion. He said, "If my men are going to be murdered, I am going over with them." He led the attack and was riddled with machine gun bullets. The colonel of the 75th from Toronto was killed also. The whole four battalions were just slaughtered. What chance have men got in a case like that?
Dieppe was in much the same category. Those young men who survived were shackled for a month, but still that does not amount to maltreatment unless they can prove that they had an incapacity to work when they got out of the prison camp three or four years later. It shows how ridiculous this whole situation is. I am sure there is not a member in this house who will not agree with me that there should be a change made in the treatment being meted out to these former prisoners of war.
The next largest group would be those young Canadian airmen who were shot out of the skies over Europe. No one would charge them with being cowardly. The very flower of our young manhood were shot out of the air by the hundred with no possible chance of anything but either being killed or taken prisoner. In some cases their comrades were picked up, marched out of prison camps and shot like dogs. Then toward the end of the war, when the Russians were getting into East Germany, these men, both army and airmen, were taken out of German prison camps and marched across the country in winter weather without any proper treatment at all. Some of the men on the staff in this building went through those experiences. Today they are trying to establish a claim under this procedure. Somebody has to prepare it for them. They have to prove maltreatment. They have to prove that when they were released they were incapacitated for work. There is delay. It is going to take months for them to get an award, and many of them will not get an award. Those who do probably will not get the amount to which they are entitled.
I plead with the minister and members of the house to change this situation and make
Supply-Veterans Affairs provision for a payment to those young Canadians who were prisoners of war without making them cut all the red tape involved under the present method of handling this problem.
Those are the four suggestions I place before the house today, Mr. Chairman. I trust that they will be of some help to my old comrades, either as a result of action now, or before the new parliament assembles, or at the first session of that parliament.

519. War veterans' allowance board-administration, $141,335.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
This item has to do with the war veterans allowance. I refrained from taking the time of the committee when we were on the first item of this department for obvious reasons. But I should like to
5128	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs * add my voice to the very effective representations that have already been made during this debate by at least fifteen hon. members with respect to the war veterans allowance. The minister must know very well-he must know them by heart; he must think of them in his sleep-the representations that have been made by the Canadian Legion in connection with this legislation; and I wish to urge once again as strongly as I can that their representations be met. They ask that the allowance be raised to $60 a month for single veterans and $120 a month for married veterans. These requests are reasonable and [responsible. They ask, too, that if the means test cannot completely be removed, at least the annual total permissible income be raised to $1,200 for a single person and $2,000 for a married person.
We have requested these changes time and again on the floor of this house. I am sure that all of us in this house feel that our burnt-out veterans have these improvements in this legislation coming to them.
I should like to support also the other representations made, particularly with reference to the widows of imperial veterans.
I will not take further time now except to say that in my view the fifteen or more members who thus far have spoken on this question in the debate on these estimates have expressed the views of hon. members as a whole, and have expressed the desires of the people of Canada that we do our very best for our burnt-out veterans.

I merely want to add my voice to those who have already spoken in favour of the veterans who come under the veterans allowance clause. The country at large is quite ready to support the department and the government in an increase in that allowance. I have the privilege of getting about the country a little. I cannot speak for the country at large, but I am quite sure I can speak for the voters of my constituency. In that constituency I would say that, regardless of the political affiliation of the voters and citizens, they would support the minister and the government in an increase in the allowance to the amounts which have been requested by the Canadian Legion.
I do not know why the minister has hesitated. I am sure it is not because the minister himself does not believe that this case merits a greater reward than it is getting. I am sure that the minister himself would, if his hands were free, increase that veterans' allowance to $60 and $120 a month, and increase the permissible income ceiling.


I just cannot understand why the department insists on sticking to that ceiling; why they insist that a single veteran must still be kept at that permissible income ceiling. That could be raised without placing any great expense upon the government or the taxpayers. I am confident that the taxpayers throughout this country would support him. I urge the minister to give that his attention.
Now, Mr. Chairman, with your permission I might refer for a few moments to something that may not be strictly in order. I shall only have to get on my feet again to say it if I do not say it now. I want to thank the department for the good work which one branch has done recently. When I spoke in this house in January on veterans affairs I called the attention of the house to the plight of a veteran in my constituency who, when his case was brought to my attention, was completely unable to work and had not been able to work for two years, and concerning whom the doctors had said his case was incurable. The man was supposed to be permanently disabled.
I find that somebody in the minister's department even reads Hansard or listens to what members of parliament say in the house, because a couple of days later I received a call from the department asking for particulars about this veteran. That was then pretty nearly in the middle of January. Before the end of January the minister's officers in Toronto had an interview with that veteran, they had him in Sunnybrook hospital and kept him there until the end of March. They had him examined by all kinds of specialists. A dozen specialists must have examined him. They placed him in a clinic, and at the end of March were able to discharge him and declared that he was capable of doing light work. But better than that, the officers found him a job, and assured me that with continued treatment and with continual review of his case the man is going to be completely rehabilitated. Here is a man who was completely helpless for two years. When I saw him he could barely shuffle around. The department took that man in charge, and I want to assure him that the man and his family are now quite happy.
I had some other comments to make, but I do not wish to transgress the rules by making any further comment at this time. May I compliment the minister's department upon the very excellent job of rehabilitation they have done. I think credit must go to the welfare officers in Toronto.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on behalf of the veterans. I am sure every veteran in the house agrees that those of us who were fortunate do not feel any ill effects from the last two wars. But we do know when we look at veterans who did suffer from their war service that there is something about serving in Her Majesty's forces, and the conditions under which the men must serve, that definitely has an effect on the health of those who do serve.
They were young men when they enlisted; but the fact is that no human beings are expected to live under exactly the same trying conditions as those under which men who are now veterans have had to live. That service has its toll. The manner in which they must live, the discipline they must follow, and the fact that young Canadians are not used to the conditions found in army life have a real effect on the man who joins the army, from the date of his enlistment until the day he is discharged. Perhaps the effect is not so apparent at the time of service when all seem to be enjoying themselves and are showing their delight in serving the country. But I do know that many of my old comrades of the first world war who, when discharged, appeared to be in good physical condition, are deserving of special consideration today; and I have no doubt their condition now is entirely due to the conditions under which they served.
I would ask the minister and his officials to keep these facts in mind and, if at all possible, to give special consideration to burnt-out pensioners. They are not lead-swingers; they deserve special consideration, and I believe the people of Canada generally would gladly meet the expense of paying extra pensions to those men. That extra amount of money would keep them in the condition to which we all feel they are entitled; and in this way we could be proud that we are doing something for those who served us so well.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add my voice to those of other hon. members who have pointed out the great need for increases in war veterans allowances. In common with many other hon. members, I have been approached from time to time by Legion branches; and it seems to me that the need for an increase in the war veterans allowance paid to persons who served in an active theatre of war in the first great war is the question most frequently raised by members of the Legion. The amount required to
Supply-Veterans Affairs increase the allowance would be very small indeed, when one considers the great sacrifice these men have made.
The government and the people of Canada could and should do much better for our older veterans. The request of the Canadian Legion that the war veterans allowance be increased from $50 to $60 a month for single persons and from $90 to $120 a month for married and an increase in allowable income to $1,200 and $2,000 is fully justified.
The veterans resent deeply the fact that when they reach the age of seventy years and receive the old age security pension they do not receive the same benefits from that pension as do other citizens throughout the country. The fact is that they do not receive an increase of $40 a month in their incomes, because their war veterans' allowance is subsequently reduced.
I do not think that is a fair procedure. Any argument that no means test is required to receive the old age security pension does not recommend itself to those who were receiving war veterans allowance. All they gain is another $10 a month. I would like to see the $40 received under the old age pension added to the present $50 paid by way of war veterans' allowance, when these persons reach the age of seventy years. And even though this session is almost ended, even though the life of this parliament is short, I contend that even at this late hour the government should grant at this session an increase in the war veterans' allowance. I have no doubt such an increase would be applauded by members in all parts of the house.
