521. War veterans' allowances, $26,373,000.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Is not the minister going to make some comment in reply to the now twenty members who have asked that the representations made by the Canadian Legion in respect of the war veterans allowance be met by the government?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I had expected at the conclusion of the discussion on the first item of my estimates that I might be called upon to make a few comments, particularly on this subject. However, the item was carried in such a hurry that I did not have a chance to get to my feet.
However, I do wish to say to the committee that I appreciate very much the representations made and the spirit in which the discussion has been conducted. These

Supply-Veterans Affairs discussions which take place when the first item in a department is called are most useful. They permit hon. members not only to examine and discuss departmental policies, but also to bring forward cases which have come to their attention in their own localities. The department is then given an opportunity to take action.
I do not wish to speak at great length, but I think all hon. members will agree that the question of war veterans allowances is much more complicated than would first appear when suggestions are made in the House of Commons. I think all the comments by hon. members in this debate might well be summed up under three headings: First, that the rates of war veterans allowances should be increased; second, that the permissible income ceiling should be raised; and third, that the means test should be taken away. Not all hon. members have supported the last suggestion, but it was brought forward by several hon. members, and has been suggested at various times before.
As regards rates, I think to be fair in discussing this question we must go back to the origin of the War Veterans Allowance Act. I do not believe there are any members here this afternoon who were members of the house at the time the act was passed in 1930. If one studies the debates which took place at that time and the reports of the committees which were looking into veterans' problems, one cannot get away from the fact that the war veterans allowance was a social measure brought forward to permit a war veteran to draw the equivalent of the old age pension at an earlier date than was provided for in the Old Age Pensions Act. This right was given because of pre-ageing brought about by service in a theatre of operations.
One hon. member has said that we have got away from this association of the war veterans allowance with the old age pension. It may be that in their own minds some have got away from that association, but the fact remains that the principle upon which the legislation was based at that time was that pre-ageing due to war service permitted the drawing of the equivalent of the old age pension. That principle has been carried through since 1930. Every time the old age pension was increased the war veterans allowance was also increased.
As I said, one must go back to the records of that day to find out exactly what took place. I find in the report of the pensions and returned soldiers' problems committee which sat in 1930 the evidence of the then deputy minister of the department, Colonel Amyot, who testified as a witness before the

committee. Having explained the pre-ageing theory, he went on to say:
Two or three years ago the minister conceived the idea of putting these men under, not the Pension Act, but under the special allowance act of the nature of old age pensions. A good deal of study has been given to it from that time, by the department, and very intensive study during the last six months, and out of that has developed this Bill 19.
That was the bill which was first introduced.
In the preamble of the bill, these ideas are included:
"Whereas there are a great number of veterans in Canada who are not in receipt of pensions under the provisions of the Pension Act-"
He then went on to explain that this social legislation was for the purpose of making available to veterans the old age pension before they had reached the age provided by the Old Age Pensions Act. The same thing was said right in this house. If one goes back to the debates of the time when the measure was introduced he will find that the then minister put forward exactly the same theory. That was accepted by everyone in the house and by the veterans' organizations who had worked very closely with the department in drafting this legislation. I should like to give one short quotation from the minister's remarks on this subject in March, 1930. The then minister, who was Dr. King, said:
The provision Is made that a soldier who has reached the age of sixty-five,-
When originally presented, the bill made provision for the allowance payable at sixty-five, but it was amended at that same session.
-if he can qualify under the provisions of the present Old Age Pensions Act, he will come under that legislation. Then, there is the provision whereby a veteran who has become disabled, and through illness or disability is not employable, is treated as though he had reached the age of sixty-five.
He would obtain a pension in the nature of an old age pension?
He would get a pension similar to the other pension.
In the nature of an old age pension?
Yes.
Or in the nature of a pension under the Pension Act?

No, an old age pension.
That principle has been accepted right from the beginning. When one wants to amend legislation of this sort it is difficult to get away from its relationship with the old age pension.
Another point made was that the ceiling of permissible income should be raised. Here again there is the same relationship between the War Veterans Allowance Act and the Old Age Assistance Act-in both cases the ceiling is the same.

However, the act was amended last year by adding a new section 4 which, as hon. members know, permits the recipient of a war veterans allowance to take temporary employment, and then when that employment ceases go back on war veterans allowance without his earnings being considered as income.
Some criticism was offered on Saturday that this section 4 had not fulfilled the purpose for which it was enacted. One hon. member quoted a return brought down to the house which indicated that only 231 recipients of war veterans allowance had taken advantage of the section. I think hon. members will agree that there is a reason for that. That section came into effect only on August 1, 1952. The type of employment contemplated by the section would be mainly summer seasonal employment. Undoubtedly during the first few months of the operation of the section only a few veterans took advantage of it. However, the number is increasing slowly and the officers of the department are quite sure that during the course of this summer a much greater number of veterans will benefit by this section. In actual practice the section will permit a veteran to earn outside income for a period of a few months without it being considered income for the purposes of war veterans allowance.
I think it was the hon. member for Royal who read a letter or article to the house which demonstrated the impossibility of a recipient of war veterans allowance doing certain types of work. The case which he put before the committee was, I think, that of a veteran who had been offered employment by the minister of the local church.
It was mentioned in the Legion brief.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I believe it was mentioned in the Legion brief. I would naturally be interested, as a matter of fact, in seeing those cases again brought before the war veterans allowance board because since section 4 came into operation a new interpretation has been given concerning the income permissible under the act. I have in mind one particular case which is quite similar to the one to which the hon. member referred. This was the case of a veteran living here in Ontario and who had been offered employment by the minister of the church in his village; he was to act as caretaker of the church and parish hall, and as furnace man during the winter, at a salary of $85 a month. He was to be responsible for cleaning out the church and that sort of thing. The war veterans allowance board, after discussion with the 68108-324
Supply-Veterans Affairs unemployment insurance commission, has established that this type of employment is to be considered as subsidiary employment or work that could be performed outside of regular working hours if the veteran was otherwise employed. I understand that is the interpretation which is given for the payment of unemployment insurance. A worker who is out of work can draw unemployment insurance and also obtain subsidiary employment if it is of a nature that he could perform in outside hours while doing his regular work, and if it provides him with an income of not more than $2 a day.
May I ask the minister this question? Does that mean that such income would be considered as casual earnings?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I suppose so.
That is the only provision there is in the act.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Yes. For instance, in the case to which I am referring, this man gets $85 per month. Of this amount, $50 is considered as subsidiary earnings which are permissible. Of the $85 which he earns, only $35 is considered as income for the purpose of war veterans' allowance. Hence he draws $85 plus $65 war veterans allowance, or $150 a month. I am just giving this case as an illustration of what can be done under section
4.	I am quite convinced that, when the operation of the section is well understood by the veterans concerned, many more will take advantage of it.
On Saturday the statement was made that there is no reason why the ceiling should not be raised as it would not cost the government of this country one dollar more. I was rather surprised to hear an hon. member make that statement, and I was more greatly surprised when the statement was repeated by none other than the hon. member for Greenwood, the financial critic of the official opposition. Anyone who has even a slight understanding of the operations of the War Veterans Allowance Act can readily see that raising the ceiling by any amount immediately brings in under the act people who are being excluded because of the ceiling, or some who are already drawing part of the war veterans allowance to draw a bigger amount. It has been estimated that if at the present time the ceiling were raised to $1,200 and $2,000-I think that was the suggestion which was made-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: That is the Legion suggestion.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
-at least 8,000 pensioners who are not now under war veterans allowance would qualify, and that at least a similar number of non-pensioners would be
5132	HOUSE OF
Supply-Veterans Affairs able to draw either the whole or part of the war veterans allowance. It can therefore easily be seen-and I am not saying this as an argument against it-that the raising of the ceiling would increase considerably the expense in connection with the war veterans allowance. I was greatly surprised to hear the statement made by the hon. member for Greenwood the other day.
It is also suggested that the means test should be taken off in connection with the war veterans allowance. I wonder if those who made this suggestion have really contemplated all that would result from, or the actual effect of, taking away the means test with respect to the war veterans' allowance. It would mean that every man in this country who at one time or another served in a theatre of operations would automatically, at the age of 60, get the war veterans allowance.
I have not at hand the exact figures with regard to the number of veterans in Canada who have served in a theatre of operations. I believe the last census in 1951 indicated that the veteran population of Canada was slightly over one and a quarter million. We know that in the second world war nearly 800,000-I think the figure is 785,000-served outside of Canada. In the first war over
350,000	served outside of Canada though, of course, a great many of them have disappeared since then. However, one can easily see the implication of putting every man automatically on war veterans' allowance upon his reaching the age of 60. I asked one of my officials to estimate what the expense involved would be. He did not have at hand all the figures necessary to give an accurate estimate, but at present it would be roughly $65 to $70 million which would be paid automatically to veterans now at age 60.
I just want to put that situation before the committee. I think it is something that should be considered. When they study the full implication of taking the means test off in connection with the war veterans' allowance, I doubt whether hon. members would think it appropriate to do it at this time.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question? He has discussed quite fully the remarks that have been made by members in all parts of the house on this matter of war veterans allowances. Apart from such matters as the regulations with respect to widows of imperial veterans he has quite fairly summed up what members have been asking for. I would just make this one comment. I think hon. members have all asked for his first point, namely an increase in the rates, and then they have asked for either the second or third, not both. After all, if 

we got the third point we would not have to worry about the second.
In the main, therefore, I make this clarification of what the minister said by way of summing up what we have asked for. We have asked first for an increase in the rates and second either for the removal of the means test or for an increase in the permissible income ceilings, in the case of single veterans from $720 to $1,200 and in the case of married veterans from $1,200 to $2,000. Having said that, this is my question: Are we to take it from what the minister has said in his remarks just now that the government is opposed to making any of these changes at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
The matter is still being considered. We have studied the matter considerably, and we have tried to bring forward some changes which have resulted from this study. As my hon. friend knows, there is no provision before parliament for any immediate changes in the act.
Mi. Quelch: I listened with interest to what the minister had to say with regard to casual earnings. To me his remarks were just about as confusing as the remarks which are contained in the little booklet which is sent out to veterans. I know an old veteran in this city who is over 80 years of age. Along with all recipients of war veterans allowances, I suppose, he receives a form which has to be filled in. It is a sort of net worth statement. Every time he receives this form he gets quite upset and worried because he thinks the government is charging him with receiving money to which he is not entitled.
I went over the form with him, and in one line there is a space for income. In another line there is "all other income" which I take to mean casual earnings. In the little booklet regarding earnings and earned income it gives an example of earned income, where a man may go out in the afternoon for an hour or so and do some carpentry. That would be earned income. However, if the man went out after hours and did some gardening, money received for it would be covered by "casual earnings". My question is this. What does "after hours" mean for a man who is not working at all? It is the most nonsensical thing I have ever heard of. If a man is not working there is no such thing for him as "after hours".
Why should you insist that a man who is 70 or 80 years must go out at night? Why should he not have that casual appointment in the afternoon or in the morning? The phrase used by the minister is the same as that used in the booklet.

The man I speak of had been doing a little bit of cabinet work. That was not his work when he was previously employed; he had another occupation. He was interested, however, in cabinet work and he gets a chance to make a few dollars now and then. If he makes it in the afternoon, according to the booklet, it is earned income. If he goes out in the evening and does a little gardening or some other job, the money can be called casual earnings. I would suggest that the booklet be dropped. When the minister says "after hours" I would tell him that for a man who has no employment there is no such thing as "after hours". Why should a man not be entitled to casual earnings for work done in the morning, the afternoon or the evening, without the requirement that money be earned "after hours"?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I am sorry if I did not
express myself clearly.
You used the same expression as the book.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry if I have confused my hon. friend. Actually what is intended by the explanation in the pamphlet to which he referred is that the type of employment must be employment which, if the veteran was working regularly, he could do outside his regular working hours. Actually he can do it in the middle of the night if he feels like it, or in the morning-we are not concerned about that-but it must be the type of employment which my hon. friend has described and which, clearly, a workingman could do after his working hours if he so chose.

Before the item carries I wish to protest against the application of the means test to veterans. If veterans had been as niggardly toward Canada through the two terrible wars that we fought as Canada has been toward them I do not know what would have happened to Canada. I cannot see any justification whatever for connecting veterans' income with the old age pension. If the veteran had never gone to war he would have received the old age pension.
Are we not endeavouring to reward these men in some measure for the devoted service which they rendered to this nation? Surely every good Canadian feels a debt of gratitude toward these men. When are we going to pay that debt of gratitude? I realize the minister's position; I realize that he and his department are bound by law, but I just cannot escape the thought that the time is long overdue when something should be done about the law. I am quite sure that nothing 68108-3241
Supply-Veterans Affairs will be done about the law until the minister says it is to be done.
I realize that men think of money as only that which is taken from the pockets of the citizens of Canada. I realize that they attach to money a sort of sanctity, and certainly the people of Canada should not be taxed beyond their ability to endure. Surely, however, there must be some way of establishing a relation between the productive capacity of this nation and its ability to reward those who have served and who are worthy of consideration.
In dealing with the veterans' problem and applying the means test to it, I would like to suggest that it would be well for us to bear in mind that once a man falls into the unhappy position of being on war veterans allowance he has no chance to buy the presents he would like to buy for his dear ones. He cannot even afford Christmas cards; he cannot afford to go to picture shows; and he cannot afford to indulge himself to a little treat in the ice cream parlour. That is his reward for offering his life for Canada, for fighting through hell. Well, surely it is time we began to adopt a proper perspective in these matters. I am not going to suggest at the moment how that can be done but I will say, before leaving the matter, that to believe there can be no money in the hands of the government other than money taken from the people in taxation is a manifestation of the crassest kind of ignorance concerning money. I find myself utterly at a loss when trying to comprehend the attitude of men who cannot realize that money is the creation of the state. It always has been since Canada was Canada. It was so before Canada was formed. What species of delusion is coming over the-minds of men today when they refuse to believe that money can be created by the state in accordance with the goods and services which the state can produce?
I merely raise that question, and before taking my seat I protest with all the vehemence of which my being is capable against the niggardly way in which we are dealing with our war veterans when they fall into the class requiring war veterans allowance.

I have not said anything about this particular department as yet, but I think one of the most important duties of a member in this house is the responsibility of looking after the needs of the veterans in this country. Before mentioning the particular item relating to pensions which I have in mind, I should like to say in passing that I do agree with the representations that have been made with regard to war veterans allowances.
I have a pension case in which I am interested, along with about six or seven other members in this house. I think that fact alone indicates the necessity of appointing a standing committee on veterans affairs.

There has been a lot of duplication of effort and activity in regard to this particular case. I am sure that as various representations are made by different members concerning pension cases, the officials of the department must become exasperated at times trying to explain, repeating the same story to each member who approaches them on the subject. I must say they do maintain a very high level of courtesy, even though they must feel that much unnecessary effort arises from this repetition of investigation.
The case is somewhat similar to that dealt with by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. It concerns a fatal accident that occurred to an officer in the R.C.A.F. The case is well known to the department. It is that of Flight Lieutenant James Olver, J-51458, who was killed at Centralia on December 11, 1951. Briefly the details are as follows: Flying was washed out that particular day. The officer returned to his quarters off the station. He was riding with another officer from Centralia station, who became involved in an accident on the way home. Flight Lieutenant Olver was killed.
Three hearings have been held on this case. Each time the verdict has been returned that the widow and family of the service man are not pensionable because the officer was not on duty at the time of his death. I want to place on record the finding of the board in this regard because it points up a suggestion that I am going to make before concluding my observations. The last hearing came to this conclusion on February 27. Briefly the pension board found as follows:
It should be pointed out this case does not appear to be unusual in that the majority of service personnel, particularly married personnel, live "off the station" and therefore away from the unit concerned and would not appear to be under service jurisdiction so far as their off duty activities, et cetera, are concerned. There may be some service sponsorship so far as deportment is concerned, but their time and their occupation, et cetera, would seem to be at their own discretion from the time they leave the unit. After consideration of the above points, this board must find death in this case was due to an accident which did not arise out of nor was it directly connected with peacetime service after world war II, and death therefore is not pensionable under section 11 (2).
The argument that has been put forward in successive hearings of course has been to the effect that the airman was actually in the course of duty because he was on his way home to his quarters. I am not going to pursue the arguments in the case here, but I am going to say that there are some pertinent observations that arise out of a problem of that kind.
As I look back on the history of pension legislation, after world war I the feeling seemed to be that provision for pensions
Supply-Veterans Affairs for service personnel was a temporary expedient. World war I was the war supposed to end all wars. There would be no further wars, and therefore the need for veterans' welfare would gradually disappear, would wither away. As I have searched the records, it seems that this attitude persisted almost to 1936, when pension legislation became more or less fixed and statutory.
In view of our experience since world war I, and particularly since world war II, we now know that it is going to be necessary for Canada to maintain fairly substantial armed forces. Because of this, veterans' problems have attained permanent status. It is quite significant, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has pointed out, that our present military establishment is made up of 40 per cent married personnel. I would suggest that if we are to have problems arising continually concerning decisions on these borderline or marginal pension cases, it is not going to be much of an inducement for Canadian citizens to make a career out of service activity.
The needs of the world, the problems of maintaining peace in the world and also providing the necessary defence measures in this country today make it necessary that we have permanent forces established. That being so, our attitude towards pensionable liability in regard to service personnel must change considerably. In the particular case to which I have referred, the case of Flight Lieutenant Olver, a widow and young daughter are left, and they have absolutely no claim at all in connection with the loss of life of the husband and father who, believing himself covered by military pension provisions, had not provided the usual civilian protection for his family. As I discussed the case with the members of the department, who have been the essence of courtesy and helpfulness, I found they could go only so far as the statutory measures allow. That would tend to suggest to me there is some need to reconsider the statutory provisions dealing with these borderline cases to make it possible to have some broader interpretation in the Pension Act in regard to death arising from peacetime service.
I come back and suggest that if we had a standing committee on veterans affairs, this is a problem to which such a committee could give some attention. Obviously if it is going to be necessary for Canadians to make a career of military service they have to know in no uncertain terms the position of their families should the breadwinner be suddenly killed whether directly in line with the course of military duties or in borderline cases such as the one I have outlined here.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I am sure the members of the department- they have never said so, but I would come to this conclusion-would support strongly the idea of a standing committee that could deal with these matters, a committee to which members of this house could go and have a free exchange of ideas on problem cases, and also where some discussion of the necessary statutory changes could take place in order to make it possible to deal in a fair and just way with these problems rather than having to say, as the board has felt obliged to conclude, that a case of this kind is not pensionable under section 11(2) of the act.

I have one small problem to bring to the attention of the minister. I will do it as quickly as I can. It involves only 200 people in all Canada so far as I know. These are widows who were married to members of the British merchant marine during the war. They have received a British pension, but apparently they cannot get it supplemented in Canada. I think that is wrong, because the amount that is received from Britain today is so small that it can hardly keep body and soul together. I ask the minister whether something cannot be done for these 200 people that I know of.

Well, the hon. member has made particular reference during the course of the debate to the claim of a widow, where death was the result of a vehicle accident during service in peacetime. The hon. member is well aware that claims such as that are dealt with under section 11(2) of the Pension Act, and in order that entitlement be conceded it is necessary to establish that death arose out of or was directly connected with service. The hon. member also knows that this parliament has given the Canadian pension commission sole authority and exclusive jurisdiction to adjudicate on all claims under the Pension Act. As minister I cannot make any comment on any of the decisions of the commission, nor can I intervene.
I believe this was wise legislation on the part of parliament. Otherwise it can readily be seen that if a minister could intervene in

any of the decisions of the commission his office would be used as an appeal court on all pension matters where applicants were not dealt with as they felt they should have been.
This legislation was passed by parliament as a result of requests by veteran groups. There is nothing more that I can say on the point.

Last year the minister was good enough to have something done about this, and I thank him for what he did. We fully realize that maintenance plays a very important part in the successful operation of a septic disposal system, but may we point out that it is impossible to keep it operational when It has not been constructed properly. By this we refer you to the previous letter we submitted and photographs of constructional defects found in all of the three fields we inspected.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
I have the photographs here which I showed the minister last year.
When we contracted to purchase these small holdings we were under the impression that they were to he fully modern and that the Veterans' Land Act itself was to assist returning men. I have a question which I have asked on a number of previous occasions. Can the department give consideration to allowing veterans who have small holdings which have been taken into municipalities to sell part of their land in order to help in the payment of the taxes which have gone up so greatly? It is almost impossible for many of these men to pay these taxes. Part of their holdings

could be sold and the money obtained from the sale turned over to the department to help pay for the property.

That is all right if the veteran is outside a city, but when his holding is taken into the city he must pay for sidewalks and other local improvements. I submit that the veteran should be allowed to sell a portion of his holding under those circumstances. I understand that if he is in receipt of pension he may sell off some of his holding as long as he retains the house in which he lives.

Mr. Chairman, I want to bring to the attention of the minister a matter that is of serious concern to a number of veterans in my constituency. I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say that I always talk briefly, reasonably and with common sense. The matter I wish to bring to his attention relates to the reduction of the acreage of small holdings.
When the acreage was raised from half an acre to three acres in most cases, there were hundreds of veterans in my constituency who were denied the opportunity of taking up small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act. This is a particularly serious problem in the district in which I live because of the topography and the shortage of land around Nelson, Trail and some other centres because of the increasing industrial development in the whole area. Because of these circumstances, year after year I have urged the department to give consideration to making exceptions in the particular circumstances that exist in my constituency.
This is of such serious concern that at every meeting of the West Kootenay zone council of the Canadian Legion during the past three or four years a resolution has been passed urging a reduction in the acreage to half an acre. It is a matter that has

caused lengthy debate and serious protest. The boys have asked me to bring this matter to the minister's attention again, and I am doing it now as briefly as possible.
What I cannot understand, Mr. Chairman, is the reason behind this raising of the acreage from half an acre to three acres. I think it is three acres in the majority of cases, although in some circumstances it is reduced to 1-6 acres and so on. I do not understand the reason. There does not seem to be any logic in it. Surely it is just denying the benefits of an excellent act to a large number of veterans.
In my opinion that section of the Veterans Land Act is the best housing scheme in Canada. Many veterans in my district have had an opportunity to take advantage of it.
I am sure the minister's officials will inform him that there are some of the finest small holding settlements in Canada right in the constituency of Kootenay West. It is a treat to visit these boys and find out what is being done. But I urge that consideration be given again to the pleas of these veterans-it is not only in my district, but I understand it also applies to other districts in Canada-to have this acreage reduced to half an acre where it is impossible to obtain any larger area of land and where on that account hundreds of veterans are being denied an opportunity of taking advantage of the act.
Just before going on to one other pet subject of mine, I want to compliment the department on the construction schools that were put into operation in Kootenay West last year. I think three schools were held, largely owing to the fact that the director visited the district and saw the need. All classes were well attended. The instructors were excellent. There was great interest among the men who derived a great deal of benefit. I understand they were taught to read plans in a rough way, to prepare a site, to assemble material, to erect a building in order, and to perform certain more or less rudimentary carpentry work. In any event, all those who took that course told me that it was an excellent one and that they hope the department will, in the future, run similar schools when other men take advantage of this section of the act. It is an excellent idea. The Canadian Legion in my district and the veterans who attended asked me to express to the minister and his officials their sincere appreciation for the operation of those schools in the district last year.
I have another pet peeve, and I think the minister may know what it is. It is not only my peeve but it is the peeve of the 68108-325
Supply-Veterans Affairs Canadian Legion in my district. Resolutions have been passed repeatedly at zone councils. I refer to the reduction of the Veterans' Land Act administration staff in the Kootenay district. We are tired of being the tail of the Okanagan dog. We are an extremely important district. I want it to be understood that, in making that criticism, we are making no criticism of the local officials. The services of the local officials have been commented upon by favourable resolutions at various veteran meetings, but they are simply overburdened with work and are unable to keep up with it. Moreover, the settlement in the area, as the minister will find if he looks the matter up, is increasing every year.
Here is the situation. You have two field officers and a man in charge of housing. The office in Nelson is open one day a week. Veterans may have to drive 150 miles. If it is not convenient to be there on Monday- I think that is the day on which it is open -they are not able to go ahead with their application or attend to their business. You cannot blame the field men. They are out in the field trying to keep up with the work. In fact it is impossible for them to keep up with the work. As I said before, and I think the director will bear me out in this, the applications are increasing daily.
When one makes an argument in cases like this, I think it is a good thing to bring concrete evidence in support of it. I intend to do that by reading two letters I have received from a very responsible veteran who is a competent pioneer farmer, a land appraiser by profession who is considered to be one of the best in the interior. In fact he is employed periodically by some of the insurance companies to appraise land and give them an opinion as to the value of the property for mortgages and so on. I read this letter:
Dear Mr. Herridge:
I am enclosing copies of a letter which I am today passing in to the Legion. I think you will find the letter self-explanatory. As far as I recall, there are about fourteen or fifteen veterans affected in a similar manner along the north shore. Two others, Mr. Charley Noakes of Balfour and Mr. A. Merz of Queens Bay have also made written complaints to the Legion at Nelson on the same subject.
As a matter of fact, the official survey of the constructed power line was made twelve months ago by B.C. land surveyor, Boyd Affleck. At that time survey stakes were set where the power line crossed each property. There was no reason therefore why an easement report could not have been completed any time after that date, and a claim for compensation filed with the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
With the usual spring rush at the V.L.A. it is conceivable that the matter will drift on for more months unless pressure is brought to bear. The point is that veterans on these V.L.A. properties are being placed at a disadvantage as compared with

Supply-Veterans Affairs their civilian neighbours, something which I am quite sure was never intended.
Please understand that this letter implies no criticism of Mr. Cooper. He is working at high pressure all the time, and in the summer puts in long hours, . . .
Then I just want to read the letter to the Legion as evidence of the need for additional staff. I might say that I think it was most unfair that the extremely competent senior official of the Veterans' Land Act department who was then in Nelson at that time was laid off. I am not alone in that sentiment. I have the support of all the Legion branches and a good number of the people in the community, including business people. This letter is addressed to the secretary-manager, Canadian Legion, at Nelson. It reads as follows:
Dear Sir:
For some months past the Nelson branch, in company with other branches of the Legion in West Kootenay, has been pressing the Veterans' Land Act administration to provide additional staff for Nelson district, in order that efficient service may be provided for veterans in this area. It is realized that in order to press such a request, concrete examples of inadequate service must be provided. The purpose of this letter is to cite such a case.
In January of 1951 the V.L.A. granted authority to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company to construct a right of way for a power line across various V.L.A. properties along the north shore in the Nelson district. It was agreed that proper compensation would be made by the company to the veterans concerned, through the V.L.A., when the line was completed, and damage to and loss of value in respect of each property could be properly assessed.
The right of way was slashed in the early spring of 1951 and the power line installed shortly after. It is now two years since this was done and civilian owners of properties affected have long since been paid compensation, but not so the veterans concerned. The explanation offered is that the skeleton staff at Nelson is so busy with more urgent business that they are unable to find time to make the necessary easement reports in these cases in order that claim for compensation may be presented to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company. This deplorable delay has thus deprived veterans of moneys to which they are entitled, for an unreasonable time.
It is difficult to understand why the administration of the Veterans' Land Act in this district cannot be organized to provide service with more efficiency and dispatch.
We are all aware that the V.L.A. can find time to make very frequent visits to veterans who are in arrears in their monthly payments to the V.L.A., even when quite small amounts are involved. Yet, when the shoe is on the other foot and the money is due the veteran, the matter can be left in abeyance for months.
It is suggested that if the V.L.A. is no longer prepared to provide the necessary staff to carry out the provisions of the act then it is high time that the regulations be revised.
It is hoped that the Legion can insist that action be taken in the matter without further delay.
In fairness to the administration, I may say that after that protest was made by my-

self and by the Legion, some extra help was sent in to the Kootenays and I think, although I am not quite sure, the matter is to be settled in the near future.
I want to bring these facts to the attention of the minister and have him compare them with those in connection with any other district in Canada. I understand the repayment record in West Kootenay is the best in British Columbia. Why? Because the production in the area served by the Nelson office was over $200 million last year. There is a sound development there, and it is becoming increasingly sound. These men who will be applying for loans are largely men employed in permanent industry at good wages or salaries. I believe it is about time that we had an increase in staff at the Nelson office in order to prepare for the future.
I want to tell the minister what the future means. There is a $65 million pulp mill to be built in Kootenay West. Extensions are to be built to the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company plant costing over $30 million. There is a dam being built at Waneta costing over $30 million. All this will mean tremendous development. There is an increasing number of veterans coming in, veterans from the Atlantic to the Pacific who are coming into the area because they realize it is developing into one of the richest areas in Canada. The tremendous industrial development will provide permanent jobs at some of the highest wages in Canada.
This movement creates an increasing demand for housing, and it is going to mean a demand for increased agricultural production. At the present time we only produce 25 per cent of the agricultural production used in the Kootenay district.
I do ask the minister and his officials to give consideration to all these facts. I would ask the department to make Nelson a district office, running under its own steam, so it can report direct to Vancouver instead of delays being occasioned by reports having to go to Kelowna and then to Vancouver, from Vancouver back to Kelowna and from Kelowna to Nelson.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I am not critical of the officials of the department. I recognize the excellent work the local officials have done; but I am somewhat of the opinion that the senior officials do not realize the position there and the need for a district office in Nelson to serve the purposes and needs of veterans now in the district and of veterans who are to come.

I have run across a case where there was no widow for the reason that the wife had divorced the veteran shortly before he died. However, there were small children, and this war service re-establishment credit would have been a great help to them. The minister's department has ruled that section 7A of the act is not wide enough to enable them to use that money for the purpose of helping those children. The money, of course, is remaining in the fund untouched; but I am wondering if there is not some way in which that particular re-establishment credit, and the credits in cases of the same type, can be used for the children.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Section 7A (1) does give some discretion to the minister. It states:
Where a male member who has deferred his application for re-establishment credit dies after discharge, but before he has used his re-establishment credit in full, his widow, or, in case he leaves no widow, his mother, if the mother in the opinion of the minister or such person as the minister may designate, was wholly dependent on the member immediately prior to his death-
I am glad my hon. friend has drawn this matter to my attention and I will certainly look into it to see if the section as it now stands does not give sufficient authority to meet circumstances such as he has mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs

Mr. Chairman, I am not endeavouring to talk myself out, but this is a new item and I think I should mention the reason for it. Under the 1939 agreement relating to the commonwealth air training plan the government of the United Kingdom assumed financial liability for pensions and 68108-325J
Supply-Veterans Affairs certain other benefits granted to trainees under the plan who were posted to R.A.F. units on completion of their training.
The liability of the United Kingdom did not extend to personnel posted to Canadian squadrons, of whom there were three in 1939 but who by 1943 numbered 38. Subsequent to the winding up of the training plan the United Kingdom minister of pensions remained liable for pensions for disability and death which had been granted to these R.C.A.F. personnel who served with the R.A.F.
The procedure was for Canada to pay these particular pensions supplemented to Canadian rates and for the United Kingdom government to repay annually to Canada the cost of the pensions at United Kingdom rates. As a result of certain general financial negotiations which took place between my colleague the Minister of Finance and the Chancellor of the Exchequer, the United Kingdom government has been relieved of this liability and Canada has assumed full financial responsibility for these pensions from just prior to the end of the 1952-53 fiscal year.

761. Post discharge rehabilitation benefits, including the training of merchant seamen and salt water fishermen pensioners-further amount required, $100,000.

I would like to ask the minister a question on this item, but before I do so I wish to make a correction in regard to a statement I made last evening. When I was speaking on the minister's estimates I made the statement that I had received some information privately. I said I had received it from the deputy minister. On thinking the matter over and on looking at the record I want to say that I did not get the information from the deputy minister but received it from another official. I wanted to say that in fairness to the deputy minister, and I want the minister to understand because I was afraid he might fire his deputy.
My question arises out of the fact that I have had some correspondence from parents of boys who were lost in the last war while on service with the navy and air force, and who have no graves. The boys were never

Supply-Veterans Affairs found and the parents have now been circularized to the effect that in October of this year a memorial will be unveiled in Britain commemorating the boys who have no known graves. The circular, of course, points out that there will be no assistance by way of transportation and so forth to enable the parents to attend that unveiling. My information is that the Queen will unveil the memorial.
I have had a couple of letters on the matter suggesting that in view of the fact that if these boys who were lost and have no known grave had returned they would have been entitled to gratuities, educational benefits and general rehabilitation, the government might consider using those gratuities and credits to assist the parents of boys who were lost in making the trip to the unveiling of that memorial.
I do not know whether the minister's department handles this or whether it is the Department of National Defence, but any information the minister might be able to give me would be appreciated.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I am not quite sure what the hon. member wants. I understood him to ask that gratuities or re-establishment credits accruing to one of these Canadians who may have disappeared during the war should be made part of his estate and accrue to his family; is that what my hon. friend wanted?

No, that is not exactly it. I
was not making this as a general request. What I said was this. According to the letters the boy was lost and has no known grave. In October of this year a memorial is to be unveiled by the Queen commemorating the loss of that group of people. The argument advanced was that, had the boy returned, he would have been entitled to certain gratuities, rehabilitation credits and so forth. He has not returned, and has no known grave.
The parents have been invited to make the trip to take part in the unveiling of the memorial. Would the government consider making part of the rehabilitation credit, that the boy would have been entitled to, available for transportation and living allowances while the family is in Britain at that ceremony? You do not have to say you are paying gratuities, but would the government help to provide transportation and living allowances for these people while in Britain for the unveiling of that memorial?

Mr. Chairman, I was not
aware of the proposal to which my hon. friend refers. I am informed that this 

memorial to which he refers is for merchant seamen, and not men serving in the armed forces. In so far as gratuities that might have been earned by men who were lost or missing during the war are concerned, those gratuities were part of the serviceman's estate, and if the parents were the legal heirs they have received those gratuities.
Will the minister give me this assurance, that he will look into the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs

I do not think it applies to

I shall be pleased to make

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think I have only one advantage over my colleagues, Mr. Chairman, and I am not sure it is an advantage. As a rule, the greater part of the discussion on the Department of Finance takes place in the course of the budget debate. It has not been usual for me, therefore, as in the case of some of my colleagues, to make a general statement dealing with the operations of the department. Its operations, I think, are all too familiar to the members of the house.

I have one or two brief comments I should like to make before we come to the actual questions. I should like to make one or two comments on the course of the Canadian dollar and the beneficial effect on the whole, as I see it, of the fact that it has come down to what I have always thought was a more normal relationship to the United States dollar. Our exporters no longer have the disadvantage, and it was a considerable disadvantage, of a premium on the Canadian dollar. There is a considerable benefit accruing to a good many of our industries, notably newsprint, base metals, livestock, aluminum and lumber, and in general we are in a better competitive selling position.
I think we ought not to forget that it is purely an accident that our unit of currency has the same name as that of the United States unit. It is not the same unit. There are well informed people who believe that we are in a more wholesome position when our dollar actually rules at about 95 or 96 as against the United States dollar. Nevertheless it gratified our pride to have it at a

premium, and I am sure it rocked back on their heels many people in the United States who could hardly understand why that could happen.
I should like to broaden these considerations just for a moment or two by pointing out that in considering the position of the dollar we should not confine ourselves wholly to the United States, but should take a broader view. I believe we should remind ourselves that finance is merely the handmaiden of agriculture, commerce and industry, and that when we come to the thing we talk so much about, convertibility, that must come as a result rather than as a cause. In other words we must do something to free the channels of trade before we can get convertibility, though once we have it in operation, of course, it operates also to facilitate the exchange of goods.
Those things are obvious and I do not propose to dwell on them further. I do wish however to take the occasion to remind the house of what I reminded it on Saturday, of the very grave situation in which the United Kingdom finds itself at the moment by reason of the fact that the United States, notwithstanding the readiness of the President and his cabinet, is not able to step forward as it would like in trade matters. I wish to put a very short extract on the record from remarks made almost a year ago by Mr. Churchill who on June 11, 1952 said this:
It is an alert I am sounding, yet it is more than an alert, it is an alarm ... I warn you that without an intense national realization of our economic position by all parties and by all classes we shall find it very hard to reach that security without which all we have achieved and all that we possess and all our glories might rapidly become nothing.
I want to tie that in briefly with the British budget presented the other day, which has a very close relationship to our welfare. I do not propose to traverse ground which has been traversed in the matter of trade but we do realize the importance to us of the United Kingdom. I read with considerable disappointment on Saturday an article by Susan Strange in the London Observer in which she gave some rather gloomy figures as to British exports, pointing out that 1952 exports were 6 per cent below 1951, and the first three months of 1953 were 2 per cent worse than the preceding three months.
Since Churchill's statement two or three important things have happened. There has been the commonwealth conference; we had the visit of Eden and Butler to Washington; but perhaps most important of all we had the
Supply-Finance
statement made only last Friday by the chancellor of the exchequer, Mr. It. A. Butler, from which I wish to quote very briefly. He said:
United States politics is interfering with formation of a co-operative trade program to save the free world from collapse.
Then later he says:
-the fundamental question is:	Can we be
strong enough to survive the ordeal that lies before us? We have shown that we are ready to make sacrifices, but what the statesmen of the free world have not achieved yet is the task of bringing our policies together and making it certain that we have a fundamental basis on which we can build.
If I may digress for a moment, Mr. Chairman, I think a practical implication of this comes to us from the fact that the wheat agreement which we have had for years has not been signed by the United Kingdom. I suppose they have come to the conclusion that, in their own interests, they have to shop around to see if they can make a better bargain. I was interested in noticing, incidentally, that while they are proposing to open the corn exchange within the next few months, some of the people who used to operate it and used to be so expert in that operation are realizing that after 13 or 14 years of bulk purchasing and fixed prices it is not going to be so easy for them to begin to operate again.
I want to quote one more word from Mr. Butler:
Referring to the "task of bringing policies together", he said:
"This is thwarted by politics on the other side of the Atlantic and a certain lack of will and decision on this side. We are doing our best to make up our side of the bargain. It is up to the other side of the Atlantic to make up theirs."
I would remind you, Mr. Chairman, that the other side of the Atlantic includes Canada as well as the United States.
I have one other comment on the British budget. When Butler practically says there has been a certain lack of will and decision on their side of the Atlantic, he is also justified in saying "We are doing our best to make up our side of the bargain," because it seems to be the consensus of opinion that whatever else may be said about the recent British budget, it is a courageous budget, and that the chancellor has gone all out to do what he indicated when he was here. When he was here, as I recall it, he spoke about "breaking out" from the shackles of the restrictions which have impeded trade so much, and his budget is an attempt to do that.
From our point of view we all recognize the immense importance of the success of that effort because in plain words it is going

Supply-Finance
to affect the British capacity to buy goods in North America; and therefore the challenge to the United States by Butler is in a very real sense a challenge to us also.
Of course the great danger which always haunts us is that the western European nations, if they are not able to trade westward, if they are not able to sell their goods west and buy in the west, will inevitably turn and face the east. There have been some instances of that already. There were . loud outcries in the United States when Great Britain did some business with the other side of the iron curtain; and yet there have been cases-there was a case in the western states with which we are all familiar-where tenders for some large contracts were called for and Britain was the lowest tenderer, and I gather turned down for no other reason than that a United States firm might be injured if that happened. If that kind of thing is going to prevail, then these grave words of Butler that I read a few minutes ago will come to be very real indeed.
I made these few remarks, Mr. Chairman, because I thought it was desirable to have them on the record. Our own welfare, of course; our own trade, our own prosperity, the convertibility of the exchanges, which would mean so much to us, depend on the action of various people, and in no small degree on our own. These are the only general comments that I wish to make. I reserve any other remarks I have to say for the different items.

I do not generally take a
great deal of time talking on the estimates of the Minister of Finance, and I am not going to take much time now; but I do want to ask one question which I think is extremely important. I was glad the minister did not make any statement when his estimates were called; for to me it is one of the most discouraging things, one of the most disappointing things, one thing that always leaves me hanging out on a limb feeling as though I had a hangover, to listen to an orthodox finance minister try to explain anything about money.
With these introductory remarks I am going to ask the Minister of Finance one thing. What policy is the government adopting to put a little value in our Canadian dollar? The reason that most of us are urging higher pensions for older people, the reason we have voted on resolutions, as we did this morning, asking for greater consideration to be given to needy persons, is not that the number of dollars they get is small but that the dollar is only worth half what

it was worth some years ago. The person who put aside a little money for his security finds now that he cannot buy as much food as he could then.
We might explain why this is so, but I do believe those who are in charge of financial policy, not in charge of budgets, not in charge of bookkeeping, not in charge of imposing taxation and checking expenditures, but those who are in charge of finance policy should tell the people of Canada what policy they expect to pursue to bring the dollar back to the place where it will buy a dollar's worth of food, a dollar's worth of clothing, a dollar's worth of anything in relation to what it bought when people put by their savings. The minister should answer that question. If he cannot answer it, then let him tell the committee that it is beyond his ability to answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps I can best answer my hon. friend by saying that in part at any rate as a result of government policies the value of the Canadian dollar has improved some 3 or 4 per cent over the last couple of years. He and I must differ, at any rate, on these matters. He said when he listened to orthodox finance ministers he was inclined to feel he had a hangover. I am sure he will forgive m# when I say that when I listen to orthodox Social Crediters I have the same sort of feeling. Therefore I think we must agree to differ on these matters.
The only difference is that while I have a hangover the minister himself is completely knocked out.

There is just one item that I wish to deal with. I have looked over the various items in the estimates and I cannot locate the exact spot on which I should make these remarks, so I am going to say what I have to say now. What I have to say deals with the ruling of Mr. Justice Locke of the Supreme Court of Canada on April 15 in the case against the Stanley Mutual Fire Insurance Company of New Brunswick in connection with the payment of income tax, and a decision was given in favour-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I suggest to my hon. friend that perhaps his remarks might be more in point when the estimates of my colleague the Minister of National Revenue are under consideration. They will be up shortly. I think they would be more in order then. That is my suggestion.

In order to get the Minister of Finance and the hon. member for Macleod on a basis which would be familiar to each of them, probably the first problem would be

to define what we mean by the value of the Canadian dollar. I imagine that when the minister said the value of the Canadian dollar had improved he meant its value on the exchange is greater. Surely he did not seriously mean that the price structure is going down materially.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It has gone down 3 or 4 per cent in the last couple of years. That is what I was referring to; yes.

If progress goes on at the rate it is going, and in the way it is going, we shall have the primary products falling in price and we shall have the cost of production of the primary products remaining where it is. To make it quite clear, we are going to have the price of wheat down and the price of barley down, and it is likely we shall not find the price of agricultural machinery going down. If this condition goes on we shall see our primary producers crucified between low prices received for their products and high prices for the things they use to produce.
I do not see very much hope in that prospect. So far as I can see, we shall bring on a depression to bring down the price structure. If we have a depression, how can we control the speed with which it develops and the distance it will go? When we get to the bottom of the depression we shall be in a condition very similar to what obtained in the thirties when, as I said a moment ago, the prices of agricultural machinery were up, the price of twine was up, the price of nails was up, everything you went to buy to produce with was at a higher price, but the products being sold by the primary producers were being sold at lower prices.
I think that is what the hon. member for Macleod really wants to know. Does the minister actually believe that, going on as we are going now, we shall have a gradual and steady recession in the price structure, until it will be down to a level comparable with what prevailed in 1946?
Is this the depression you have been expecting for the last ten years?

Is the hon. member
serious? Was he just trying to be facetious?

I was just asking a question.
You have been talking about this depression for ten years. Is this the one we have been hearing about?
Is the minister prepared to answer my question?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If the hon. member for
Lethbridge wants me to indulge in the art of prophecy, and to say whether prices will
Supply-Finance
gradually recede to the 1946 level, I would reply that I have not the faintest idea. I personally believe that the ideal situation under existing conditions is stability of prices. I think a sharp price movement either way could cause a dislocation in the economy which would be extremely difficult to take. My personal hope is that we are in for a period of relatively stable prices.

If that proves to be so,
then what we have actually accomplished as a result of the financial and economic policy in Canada is a definite depreciation in the value of the Canadian dollar to the extent of about 48 per cent, since 1946; and we propose to stabilize at that point. Am I justified in drawing that conclusi<m from the minister's remarks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend wish me to answer? Is he asking a question?
Yes. At what point does the minister propose to stabilize prices?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I would not want to attempt
to pinpoint any particular level.

The minister has been at
so many of these conferences and participated in so many reports he has become so completely vague it is impossible for anyone to get anything from what he says.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: At least these conferences have produced some advantage, Mr. Chairman.

We have not seen any evidence of it thus far. I do not know where you would find a gloomier picture than was painted for the House of Commons the other day in the report of the Prime Minister on the result of the meeting at Washington, and the information read into the record by the hon. member for Greenwood concerning the opinions of Mr. Butler in Great Britain.
The general feeling in this House of Commons, and apparently in Great Britain, is that there is only one possible solution to the ills of our world, and that is that the United States must lower her tariff barriers and relax import restrictions to the extent that we can send enough goods into her markets to balance our trade. That seems to be the general concept of both Canada and Great Britain. If I am wrong I would be glad to have the minister set me right.
Now, if that is the general position, then it seems to me that possibly we ought to recognize, and recognize right now, that it is not at all likely that the United States will reduce her tariffs, nor oblige us by a relaxation of import restrictions to any material extent. In other words the United States is not going to let us send goods into

Supply-Finance
her economy to displace those of her own producers, or seriously to mar their welfare. This means that our desire, and the desire of Great Britain, is going to be frustrated. And if that is the only possible way out of the difficulty in which we find ourselves, then we are not going to have that way.
What we all want to know is this. What has the minister in mind as an alternative?
Nothing.

Certainly that is a question which any responsible minister and any responsible member of parliament, facing realities as they are, not the way we imagine they should be, should ask himself. That is the question to which we should receive an answer, and a rather specific answer, at that.
For example, would the minister recommend the re-establishment of imperial preferences? Would he be willing to recommend the adoption of something similar to the Ottawa agreements, signed by members of the commonwealth in 1932? I think that is a fair question, and I think the minister is the one to answer it. Has he anything to say on that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Well, if my hon. friend is asking what has been done in order to improve Canada's trading position, I do not know that the committee would wish me at this point to embark upon a review of the numerous actions taken in the last ten or fifteen years to expand Canada's trade on a multilateral basis. We have negotiated trade agreements with a great many countries, both under the original Geneva agreement and those at Annecy and Torquay, which have resulted in a very great expansion in our trade.
I do not share the hon. member's pessimism as to the future. I believe that we shall continue in the future, as we have in the past, to trade extensively with the United States, with the United Kingdom and other members of the sterling area, and with other trading nations of the world.
He has asked me a specific question, as to whether I would be in favour of expanding the imperial preference, extending the Ottawa agreements. My answer is in the negative. Our tariff schedule now contains substantial preferences in favour of the United Kingdom and sterling area countries, as well as other commonwealth countries, and I have heard no suggestion that those preferences should be abrogated. If the hon. member is asking for my personal view, then I would say I think it would be undesirable at this time to attempt to expand that preferential system.

The question that arises in the mind of any realistic man is this. Why the extreme importance that seems to be attached to the refusal by the United States to admit Canadian cheese, and several other commodities? Why all the earnestness in going to Washington recently, if we feel we can solve our problems without the United States? Why was there all that extraordinary earnestness? Would the minister explain that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I doubt very much whether the administration item of the Department of Finance is the proper place to engage in a general discussion on Canada's trade policies. I said a moment ago that I do not share my hon. friend's pessimistic views as to what will happen with respect to our trade with the United States, or with other countries.
Between all trading countries there are differences of opinion. The United States congress has taken certain action with respect to the exclusion of some of our dairy products, which we feel is injurious to our economy. Appropriate protests have been made against that action. They are being considered by the United States administration; and I have no doubt that, as has always happened in the past, the United States people and congress will be most unwilling to take any action which is unfriendly to Canada.

I am glad to have the
minister say that he doubts this is the place in which to have a general discussion on this matter of trade. I wonder if the minister would enlighten us as to where we should discuss that matter. When we raised it on the estimates of trade and commerce we were told that the Department of Trade and Commerce had nothing to do with determining policy with respect to trade. Who is responsible for determining policy? Is not the Department of Finance responsible?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance has
a special responsibility with respect to the tariff. When changes in the tariff are made they are introduced by the Minister of Finance. My hon. friend speaks generally of trade. Certainly the Minister of Trade and Commerce has greater responsibility than I in promoting the external trade of Canada. I am surprised to hear that there was any unwillingness on his part to discuss trade policies on his estimates. I think my hon. friend must have misunderstood some statement that was made.

I suppose probably the
tariff does have a great deal to do with

trade. Would the Ottawa agreements or an agreement comparable to the Ottawa agreements be the result of a recommendation by the Department of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not say, as I was not here when the Ottawa agreements were entered into. I think they were recommended by Mr. Bennett.

I imagine that he was
minister of finance at that time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes, he doubled as prime
minister and minister of finance; that is true.

And did a remarkably
good job, too. I think the further we get away from Mr. Bennett the more we shall realize the greatness of his statesmanship.
Oh, oh.

If loud retorts indicate a vacant mind, there are plenty of them over yonder. After all, I was expressing my own opinion, not necessarily the opinion of the hon. member for Jasper-Edson. I think the agreement with the British commonwealth would come under the Department of Finance. I imagine the minister has gone just about as far as he is prepared to go. He is delightfully vague as usual about this whole matter. But he leaves the Canadian people dangling pretty well in the air.
As I pointed out the other night when we were considering external affairs, we have an adverse trade balance with the United States of something over $700 million a year. Is that extreme? I think not. How long can we as a nation continue to do that? Up to the present time we have obtained the United States dollars with which to balance that adverse trade balance from Great Britain, certain sterling countries and some others. Where did they get the money with which to pay us? In large measure they got the money through such measures as the Marshall aid plan. There were several areas to which the United States granted Marshall aid, and then agreed that a considerable portion of that money should be used by the recipients of Marshall aid to buy Canadian wheat and other Canadian exports, which gave us dollars which the United States had advanced under Marshall aid.
Have we any assurance that the United States is going to continue for any considerable period of time to make such advances under Marshall aid and earmark enough of them as being eligible for expenditure in Canada to buy our wheat? Is the United States likely to continue doing that for a long enough period of time to enable us to go on buying from the United States to the
Supply-.-Finance
extent of an adverse balance of $700 million a year, and paying that back with moneys advanced by the United States, taxed or borrowed from her people?
I do not know whether the minister is optimistic enough to think she will. Suppose she does not. Suppose she stops. Then by what means do we propose to balance our trade with the United States? The minister may not wish to divulge what is in his mind in connection with this matter, but I submit that this is a vitally serious question to every Canadian. We could discuss nothing of more extreme importance right now than this very matter. I think the minister will agree that that would come under his department and this general item. The minister has nothing to say on it.
Carried.

We want to carry anything that is bothering us a little. If there is one all-important thing in the general management of the financial affairs of this country it is that which we have put our finger on. Not only are we running into an adverse trade balance with the United States in respect of the goods we import as against the goods she accepts from us, we are running into an adverse trade balance by reason of the extensive investments the United States is making in our country. What has the minister in mind to do about that?
Just as an illustration take my own province, in which we are all deeply interested. Is it not almost a national calamity to Canada that nearly all the money that financed the vast oil development in Alberta came from the United States? That money constitutes a debt to the United States which we shall have to service with United States dollars. Where are we going to get those dollars? Not only have we that vast oil development; we hear also of the development of iron ore that is contemplated by United States capital and which will also saddle upon this nation a dangerous accretion of debt.
There are extensive investments of United States capital in many of our business enterprises. Great numbers of Canadian securities are now in the hands of United States holders. Every single one of those investments constitutes one more contribution to the financial millstone around our necks which ultimately will sink us. I hope the minister can give us something that will allay the fears of informed Canadians in respect of all these matters.

I believe these charts will give a summary of the essential figures involved in the whole vexatious and anxious problem about which the minister is worrying as much as are the rest of us, and which I was referring to before we took recess.
I should like now to point out this situation. With all these deficit balances on our trading account plus the interest and sinking funds, etc., which Canada must pay to United States investors whose holdings are enumerated in the first chart I submitted, I ask the minister and the government again what policy has the government in mind in order to extricate Canada from these pressing debts, bearing in mind that their payment must be made in United States dollars or in gold?
United States dollars can be obtained only by selling goods to the United States. The disposition of the United States to accept our goods is going to be less favourable as the days go by, as that great nation approaches self-sufficiency. One of the main reasons why that great nation is going to hesitate to take many of our goods is that they are mortally afraid of the onslaught of a depression and unemployment. In 1935-this is just a little bit off the subject, but it shows exactly the kind of thing that is in the minds of many Americans who are best informed-the United States had 23,500,000 people on relief and 15 million unemployed. They do not want to get into any such condition as that
again. They are in danger of doing it if there is an amicable settlement between us and communism. They know they were in danger of descending into that condition before the Korean war started. They do not want in their country any goods which are going to put people on the unemployment rolls in the United States. Every bit of goods we ship into the United States, and which they could make, will put unemployed on their rolls. Surely we as Canadians must face that fact. They are in a position to become largely self-sufficient.
Bearing all this in mind, everyone must realize that the question I have raised is of most vital moment to every person in Canada, and to our children and their children's children yet unborn.
I feel the time has come to start on this problem right now. If we cannot pay our adverse trade balance with the United States now, we shall be less able to do so in five years. The whole nation of Canada is now mortgaged almost to the hilt to the United States, and the United States could foreclose.
I will ask the minister this question, and there is no need for him to try to answer it because he cannot do so: How in the world would you deal with the situation if they did foreclose? Obviously the first thing to do now is to stop importing from the United States the things we can get from elsewhere. If United States investments are embarrassing us and putting us into a bondage impossible to get out of, surely it is high time we
