began to limit the investment of United States capital in Canada. We must find a way to do it, but it can be done.
I think I shall just leave that question. I will not embarrass the minister by asking him to answer. I know of the difficulties with which he is confronted almost as well as he knows them, even though he is in his present position and has had much experience with it.
I know the minister is desirous of getting his estimates through the committee. If the minister would prefer it, I shall be pleased to defer a number of other things I should like to say on this occasion, if he will just allow this particular item to stand until he gets the rest of his items through and will let me speak at that time. Then we shall not be delaying the whole progress of the house and worrying the minister. Does the minister agree with that? Can we let this item stand until the rest of his estimates are through and then let me go on to say the things I want to say?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think it might be better to proceed as we have in the past, dealing with the administrative item first and then going on with the other items. I know my hon. friend always has a number of points that he wants to bring forward on this item. I think probably it would be as convenient for the committee to deal with them now as later.

Well, Mr. Chairman, first may I say I do believe there is a way out, but the trouble is that we have not begun to use the way out. I shall refer to the province of Alberta. In 1935 the debt situation in Alberta looked absolutely impossible, but today in that province we are completely free from debt. Well, how was it done?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
speechtext: They shifted it to the municipalities.

Oh, but the municipalities would have increased their debt, no matter what may have been done by the government. Besides, our increased municipal debt is carried at a low rate of interest, 2 per cent for a 20-year term. If those municipalities had borrowed in New York they would have been paying 5 per cent interest.
I would just like to have a right good-I do not know exactly what word I should use but I would like to take the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys to the mat. I tell him that in respect of all his talk against Alberta I can reduce him to mincemeat. He has not a leg to stand on, and he is standing in the light of his own province, a thing which is a shame for any member from that province to do.
The situation in Alberta in 1935 looked as impossible as the situation in the rest

of Canada now does, but by wise and courageous measures we cleared ourselves. I may tell the committee that, by the use of monetary techniques which had already been used in Canada before the day of the Bank of Canada, we can deal with these vexatious problems and extricate ourselves from this dangerous debt situation within a surprisingly short time. I could tell the committee how it can be done but I have not time to do that tonight. It would take quite a long time.
Now, then, if the minister desires to go straight ahead I want to put before him three or four more problems. I want to ask him whether the people of Canada face indefinitely an appalling housing situation such as afflicts us today. Can he conceive of no way of advancing loans for the building of houses other than through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation? Is that the best he can do when money could be made available at 1-J per cent? We are holding people up at the scandalous rate of interest which mortgage organizations are charging, 5J per cent, when Alberta alone has put herself in the position where she can lend at 2 per cent. What on earth is the matter with the Minister of Finance of Canada?
He looks pretty good.

Yes, he looks pretty good until you know about his deficiencies, and I am giving you some of them. They do not all belong to the minister, and I will say this for him! I believe he has administered the financial affairs of Canada as well as any of his predecessors since Sir Thomas White. The blame should be given to the inadequacy of the monetary instrument he is dealing with. It is not lack of skill on his part, or of ability or of integrity or any of the other fine qualities that make a minister of finance. It is the fact that he is bound by restrictions -restrictions by which he has no right to be bound, restrictions placed on him by this House of Commons in 1934 when it established the Bank of Canada.
May I return to the housing problem? Surely anyone can see that it is just grotesque, that it is fantastic, that this nation should be afflicted with a housing situation such as now prevails.
The minister has already confessed that the price structure is quite beyond him. I would like to ask him next if the people of Canada have to settle themselves down to a taxation burden like the one we are now enduring, something which constitutes downright oppression and tyranny the like of which no Anglo-Saxon people in this world have ever before endured. Can he offer any way out of that? If he cannot he is a complete

failure, or the system behind him is; and it is the system. We cannot neglect this taxation outrage.
Then we have a defence situation which is filling every Canadian with anxiety and apprehension. Last night, I think, I heard over the radio a report to the effect that General Ridgway before very long is going to make an announcement which will almost paralyse us all, telling about the inadequacy of the NATO organization in Europe. We should have been putting forth our efforts to building up the British commonwealth to what it was in 1914, which we could have done. Instead of that we have neglected the British commonwealth and all the splendid capacity it had because we have been following after one of the alphabetic monstrosities of our time, this NATO, which is only, as I say, a mirage.
Now, is the minister prepared to do anything about that? Does he see anything he can do? I ask him to be rather specific. Does he see anything he can do to build up the British commonwealth and restore Britain to her former fighting strength? He knows what she needs. She needs something to take the place of the foreign investments which she lost in two world wars for us. She needs something which will give her goods for which she does not have to trade other goods. Now, is there any man in Canada, including the Minister of Finance, who says it is physically beyond the power of Canada to help Britain back on her feet and to regain the fighting strength she had in 1914? For him to say it is, is for him to be just utterly unrealistic. All the minister needs to do is use the financial and monetary system in Canada in an intelligent and forwardlooking way to make what is physically possible for Canada financially possible.
Again the international trade prospect is far, far from encouraging. The other night the Minister of Trade and Commerce gave a fine, glowing foreign trade speech in glittering generalities. When I began to probe into the details behind the general statement he had nothing to say. He could not give a detailed answer in respect of any one of these glowing prospects which were deceiving him like a glittering mirage on the desert. There must be a way out of our trade situation. Our fundamental need is to sell goods abroad. Well, we sold goods abroad under the Dominion Notes Act of 1868 during world war I and under the Dominion Notes Act and the Finance Act of 1914, both passed by this house. Under those two acts the Dominion of Canada through the Minister of Finance, Sir Thomas White, printed $50 million
Supply-Finance
worth of debt-free and interest-free currency. With that currency the government bought $50 million worth of Canadian goods and gave the goods to Britain without interest and without debt.
Will anyone pretend for a second that the same device could not be used today to sell abroad as much goods as Canada found it necessary to sell abroad, in excess of those goods for which she could accept goods? The story is all told in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada published in 1933, page 22, paragraph 47. May I suggest that the minister get all his departmental officials or enough of them- and not the ones from the London school of economics, for they are no good at all- and have them read paragraph 47 of this report. Then they should read Sir Thomas White's comments on the findings of the commission which were forced on Canada against the better judgment of Beaudry Leman and Sir Thomas White, who were the best informed men on finance in Canada. Read what Sir Thomas White said about this matter on pages 85 to 91. I should like to read into the record a good many of the things he said. He said the devices that were used during world war I were not by any means inflationary; they were sound. The Right Hon. W. S. Fielding says almost the same thing at page 23 of the report. If the minister must keep graduates of the London school of economics around him, well let him put them to school under someone who can face the realities as the realities are. The international trade problem is not impossible to solve.
Let me ask one other question to bring it to the minister's attention. It is rumoured today quite definitely, I understand, that the steel companies intend to ask for an advance in the price of steel, starting in the United States. Undoubtedly that will be followed with a similar request in Canada. Let me say, Mr. Chairman, for about the tenth time in this house since I have been here, that the present so-called inflation in this country was induced largely by an advance of $5 a ton in the price of steel in 1946. Then the consequent strike of steel workers forced up wages. There is no answer to that statement. I say that if we have another advance in the price of steel we shall have another dangerous rise in prices, which will further cut down the value of the Canadian dollar.
What would the minister do in case there was a request for an increase of $5 per ton in the price of steel? What would he do about that? Would he let that go on, as he did in 1946 or as his colleagues forced him to do, bringing on another terrible rise in

Supply-Finance
prices and cutting down the value of the Canadian dollar another 50 per cent? Would he do that or would he know something he could do about it? Social Credit would know.
The minister could meet the situation with debt-free money issued under an act like the finance acts of 1914 and 1923, which acts were thrown into the discard by the passing of the Bank of Canada Act. That is the great crime that was committed against Canada, the passing of the Bank of Canada Act! This power of creating money which the dominion government had exercised ever since 1868, was rendered unavailable to the finance minister by the passage of the Bank of Canada Act in 1934. Apparently the people who passed the act were not aware of the terrible damage which was being done.
Now, I do not imagine that a London school of economics graduate would do anything but laugh about that, and feel quite smart; but he would just be foolish. One of the greatest disadvantages we have in Canada is that we are guided too much by the graduates of the London school of economics. Sir Thomas White knew more about finance than all the graduates of the London school of economics we have in Canada. He went through about eight years of financing, and he financed world war I. He tells about it in the report of the commission on banking and currency in Canada. Why do not the Conservatives of Canada read about it and tell us about the achievements of their great finance minister, Sir Thomas White?
We have another good one coming on now. We are all ready to take over.

You had better indicate it by your words. There is no evidence from what any Conservative speaker has said on the floor of this house in the last eight years that the Conservatives know one single thing different from that which is being carried on by the Minister of Finance. They have not anything to offer at all. They only have a lot more of what we have too much of already.
We are not trying to put him through school. We took it for granted he had been there. We are all ready.

You are all ready until you get into position. Now those are all questions which any responsible member in this house ought to ask of the minister, and to which he ought to have an answer.
I had thought of going into considerable detail concerning how these various problems, could be solved. Let me just give attention

to one or two. Suppose we have to deal with the problem of United States investors. I ask you, Mr. Chairman, this question, and I shall ask it of the minister straight to his face. Is there any reason under the sun why the money which discovered and developed oil in Alberta should not have come out of the Bank of Canada?
No answer.

There is no answer. Ask your London school of economics graduates, and what will they say? They will say that it could not possibly come out of the Bank of Canada. We just had to have United States capital come in here. We have to have it come in here to develop our iron resources. What nonsense! Back in the days of Sir Thomas White, and away back beyond that in 1868, men knew better than that.
Let us take this matter of clearing ourselves of the serious financial difficulty as regards the United States in which we are now. Suppose that we were to take the wonderful coal fields in Alberta and, by using national credit, were to develop those coal fields so that we could generate electricity from them. Supposing national credit were used and the coal fields of Alberta were developed in such a way as to produce electricity, and that development were so managed that the electricity could be introduced into the United States on a competitive basis, there is enough energy in the coal fields of Alberta to extricate this nation completely from debt within 15 years if the national credit were wisely used. That is what Social Credit could do. It would not be repudiating debts or doing anything else injurious to anybody. It would be a matter of using the financial techniques which are known to men today and could be used by men to the advantage of this nation.
I think I shall say no more at the present time. I may have a little more to say later on. In closing I urge everybody with any responsibility in Canada to look into the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada. Do not listen to those Englishmen who came over from London to sit on the commission, and who were apparently put there to enslave this nation financially. Do not depend on them. Listen to the two great Canadians on the commission, Beaudry Leman and Sir Thomas White. Read what they had to say. They told us that the Bank of Canada was going to be in, the way, that with it we would not be as able to cope with the difficulties which were going to confront us. Look at what has happened. I venture to say that the Bank of Canada has not done one thing for

Canada that was not done by the Department of Finance under Sir Thomas White, and done just as well as the Bank of Canada ever will do it. To have traded the power to create debt-free money for the Bank of Canada was certainly a fatuous deal. It was selling this nation down the river. Until we redress the wrong committed when we passed the Bank of Canada Act, we cannot get out of these various difficulties I have asked about. If we do redress that wrong, we can get out of the difficulties.

Mr. Chairman, there are one or two general questions which should be asked before we leave the first item. Will the minister say a word about the size of the staff compared with a year ago? While he is on his feet, will he also answer this? I understand that his staff is well over 4,000. I have asked this question before, but with such a large organization has he thought it well to get outside efficiency experts to consider the organization of these 4,000? It seems like a lot to organize.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The contemplated increase in the coming year over the past year is 21. The total last year was 4,886, and by far the greater number, of course, are on the staff of the comptroller of the treasury. As my hon. friend appreciates, that is a large staff because the comptroller has officers in every department of government, including the House of Commons. The contemplated total this year is 4,907. If I may say so, I think that increase is rather modest, considering the largely expanded volume of work, due in part to the Old Age Security Act which came in last year. It is pointed out to me also that the expanding volume of work in connection with defence has affected it.
Will the minister say a word on the other part of my question, whether he has sought any outside assistance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, I have not enlisted any outside assistance. My own view is that the personnel section of the treasury board itself is a pretty competent section. It is the section under the assistant deputy minister in charge of the treasury board side of the operation of the department which, in collaboration with the civil service commission, exercises direction and control over the civil service personnel, and I have never felt that up to the present we needed any people outside.

The minister realizes that I am not in the least critical, but having had some experience with a very much smaller organization, may I say that we did think it worth while from time to time
Supply-Finance
to get somebody to come in from the outside and have a look in order to get a fresh outlook.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As my hon. friend knows, we have had outside assistance in several departments, as a matter of fact in the Department of National Defence, the film board and some others. There have been reports, and I am informed that we use the organization and methods unit of the civil service commission for the purpose of making a constant review.

When these estimates were under discussion a year ago the question of the commodity prices board came up. I do not know whether this is a proper place to discuss it, but at that time we contemplated that it might be dissolved by this time. I do not find an item for it in the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are asking no vote for that organization this year, and the application is now in hand for the surrender of its charter.

I am not going to ask a question, but to make an observation. It amazes me that with 4,000 men the Minister of Finance cannot put their brains all together and answer the hon. member for Lethbridge.
(Translation):
I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) if the federal government intends to issue bilingual cheques in Canada? If so, are they distributed in all provinces or only in a few?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, bilingual
cheques are, at this time, issued in the province of Quebec only. This question of bilingual cheques is a very difficult one and, as I said to the delegation I received the other day, bilingual cheques will be issued in the other provinces as soon as circumstances will allow.
Bilingualism is spreading rather rapidly throughout this country. It goes without saying that I am in favour of bilingualism and as it was firmly established in this country without giving rise to any annoying problems, I hope that the same policy will be followed in the future.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to thank the Minister of Finance for his answer; however, he will certainly not be surprised if I say that it does not satisfy me. Bilingualism must exist everywhere in Canada and I take this opportunity to protest vigorously against the injustice being done to a million French Canadians living outside the province of Quebec.

Supply

Finance
Our constitution does not provide any exception for the province of Quebec in the matter of bilingualism. Both languages are official everywhere in Canada, from coast to coast, be it in regard to money orders, stamps or banknotes.
I do not know of anybody in Canada, whether of English, Scottish, Chinese or European origin, having refused federal government cheques because they bore a French inscription. Therefore, I would ask the minister to issue bilingual cheques not only in the province of Quebec, but in all provinces of Canada in order to place the two great races of this country on an equal footing.
I do not want to lengthen unduly this debate, but I wish to say to the minister that the delegates who came to see him recently in that connection may have been satisfied with his reply, but I certainly am not. It adds nothing to what we already knew. The minister who fulfils his mandate in a remarkable way, who represents a Montreal constituency and is well conversant with the situation of French Canadians in our province and in the country, should be the first to ask that bilingual cheques be issued not only for the citizens of the province of Quebec, but for all the citizens of our country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have listened very carefully to my hon. friend's remarks. For the moment, there is nothing I can add to what I have already said.
(Text):

I did not intend to take part in this debate at this stage at all, but in view of the question which has been put to the Minister of Finance by my confrere, the hon. member for Chicoutimi, I would be remiss in my duty, representing as I do the French Acadians of the province of New Brunswick, if I did not rise to protest in the most energetic manner against the injustice which is being meted out by this department, or by this government, to over a million French Canadians throughout Canada.
It is all very well for the minister to rise in his place tonight, in answer to a question put to him by the hon. member for Chicoutimi, and say, as he said in French a moment ago -and I must congratulate the minister for answering the hon. member for Chicoutimi in fluent French-"I received a delegation". We know that. "And I told the delegation that this was a very difficult question." The minister also told this delegation that there was no objection of any technical nature to the issuing of bilingual cheques in the Dominion of Canada, not alone in the province of Quebec.
Why, Mr. Chairman, make a special reserve of the grand old province of Quebec, and

neglect the rights of the rest of the Frenchspeaking people of Canada? I stand to be corrected if the Minister of Finance did not say to this delegation that there was no technical objection to the issuing of bilingual cheques. I stand to be corrected; but I point out to the minister-perhaps he already knows it-that in my province of New Brunswick, according to the official statistics, there are 100,712 of my people who speak nothing but the French language. In my province of New Brunswick there are also 96,095 who speak mainly French. But I wish to underline for the attention of the minister, and this government particularly, that there are in the province of New Brunswick over 100,000 French Acadians who speak nothing but French. And what about Manitoba? And what about Ontario? What about the French Acadians of Nova Scotia, of Prince Edward Island, of Newfoundland?
English.
What about them?
Who said they speak English? And what difference does it make if they do speak English?
The Acadians of Nova Scotia speak English as well as French.

I think I am an Acadian, and I speak English as well as French. But this does not take away our right to have our constitutional rights respected. Because we are able to speak both languages I do not think we should be blamed either in this House of Commons or anywhere else. I believe any man who possesses knowledge of and can speak two languages is worth two men. And that is more than my hon. friend over there, who has just interrupted me, can say for himself.
Mr. Chairman, there are 300,000 Frenchspeaking Acadians, French-speaking Canadians, in the maritime provinces, including Newfoundland. And again I say, what about Manitoba? What about Ontario? Are we going to be debarred from our right to have bilingual cheques just because this government sees fit to issue such cheques only in the province of Quebec?
I was not a member of the house but I remember reading Hansard of 1930. Let the Minister of Finance go back to 1930, to 1932, to 1933 and to 1936, and read the very able and eloquent speeches made in this House of Commons by some of the leaders of his own party. Let the Minister of Finance read the speeches made in this House of Commons by my late predecessor, the Hon. P. J. Veniot, who was postmaster general at the time he introduced bilingual stamps in Canada. Let him read, I repeat, the famous speeches made

in this House of Commons by his Liberal predecessors who put up such a brilliant defence of the universal bilingual character of Canadian money. And I submit-
And you voted against him.

I was not a member of the house at the time. Had I been here I would have voted for it. Mr. Chairman, I submit that bilingual money consecrated the principle of universal bilingualism in Canada, and that is in the very domain where Canadian cheques constitute an integral part. There is no argument which will convince me, nor will there be any argument which will convince the French-speaking people of Canada, that the Minister of Finance or this government can now refuse the issuing of bilingual cheques throughout Canada, and reserve them for the province of Quebec alone.
Had I been better prepared I could have made some further remarks on the premises I have just established. But, Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat I wish to conclude by reading an article which appeared in Le Droit of April 21, 1953. This article contains a resume of the arguments which, had I the time, I could place before you tonight, in favour of the immediate issuing of bilingual cheques throughout Canada.
It is all right for the Minister of Finance to stand up in his wizardly way and say, "Oh, we are giving this matter great and grave consideration, and probably it will come". We are not satisfied with that. We believe the time has come, indeed the time is past, when bilingual cheques should have been issued throughout Canada. I well remember some years ago when the French people in my province made a drive to have the T. Eaton Company issue French catalogues in New Brunswick. Oh, at first we were told that they would not distribute French catalogues east of Matapedia. We protested; and we finally induced them-because we had a good case-to give the French people of my native province French catalogues.
Now, if the T. Eaton Company-which, after all, is but a company-could be induced by our argument to give us French catalogues, why cannot our federal government be likewise persuaded to issue bilingual cheques throughout Canada? I can hear hon. members, especially those from the province of Quebec, going out on the hustings within a few weeks and posing as the great patriots of Canada when they address French meetings. But I say to them tonight: Why don't you rise, you Liberal members from Quebec, and support the hon. member for Chicoutimi,
Supply-Finance
if you do not want to support me, and urge upon your government the issuing of bilingual cheques. If 80 French-speaking members in this House of Commons would rise and unite as one, then I am sure the government could not resist and we would have bilingual cheques in Canada, as we are entitled to have them.
How do you like that, Fergie?
You will always hear the loud noise from the cracked bell. Keep on clanging.

I wish now to quote two paragraphs which appeared in Le Droit. With the permission of hon. members I shall read them into the record. They say:
(Translation):
There are not two kinds of French Canadians.
Because the issuing of bilingual cheques by the federal government raises a question of principle, it is impossible for us to budge from the position we have taken: we do not and cannot accept that federal cheques be bilingual in Quebec and unilingual in the rest of the country. We demand bilingual cheques for all provinces, for the French Canadians are at home and enjoy the same rights everywhere in their country. On the federal plane, we refuse to admit that Canada is an English country with one bilingual province.
In denouncing what we call "linguistic apartheid", we have nothing against any person in particular. We are fighting against a theory and a system. We are opposed to any restrictive interpretation of bilingualism, an interpretation which actually denies French Canadians living outside Quebec the rights which are recognized in the old province. When they go outside Quebec, French Canadians do not lose their nationality. The same sections of the constitution which guarantee the rights of the French language and the same measures which ensure their implementation must apply as well outside as inside the province of Quebec. There are not two kinds of French Canadians, neither are there two interpretations of the same constitutional texts.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, I leave as my last word by way of recommendation to the minister and the government, the translation of these last words from the above quoted paragraph: "There are no two kinds of French Canadians; neither are there two interpretations of the same constitutional texts".

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have listened with interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from Gloucester. I would remind him that bilingual money and bilingual stamps were introduced by a Liberal government, not by a Conservative government.
That is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I appreciate that. I am one who believes in bilingualism, and I practise what I preach. Unfortunately I do not speak French as well as I speak English, though I speak French pretty well.

Supply-Finance
The growth of bilingualism in Canada, I am happy to say, has been fairly rapid. It has my full support, as I said a few moments ago in reply to the hon. member for Chicoutimi; and my own hope is that more and more Canadians whose mother tongue is English will learn to understand and speak French. The constitutional position, which no one knows better than my hon. and learned friend from Gloucester, is that the French and English languages are official in the province of Quebec and in the parliament of Canada.
And in the Supreme Court of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
From a purely constitutional standpoint, French is not official in any other province of Canada. As I say, I am happy that the use of the French language has been extended to other provinces. There are French-language radio stations in other provinces of Canada. I am one who is happy to see that that has taken place.
Personally I deprecate making questions of this kind political issues, because I do not think they should be political issues. Unfortunately they are questions which can arouse emotions rather than reason. In answering the hon. member for Chicoutimi I said that good progress has already been made in extending bilingualism into other parts of Canada. My personal belief is that that can be effected much better and more in the interests of Canadian unity by persuasion than by violent speeches on one side or the other of this house.
My hon. friend is quite right when he says there is no technical objection to extending bilingualism to other parts of Canada. Of course he will appreciate that there is a difference between cheques and instruments like postage stamps. One cannot stop the use of money or stamps at the boundary, let us say, of the province of Quebec. I told the delegation which came to see me that I hoped and believed that the use of bilingual cheques would be extended throughout Canada as soon as circumstances would permit. I should hope that that might be achieved without raising controversies which would not be in the interests of Canadian unity.

Mr. Chairman, I listened intently to the speech of the hon. member for Gloucester. I do not think I am wrong in saying that he was daring members from Quebec to support the motion made by the hon. member for Chicoutimi and himself. All Liberal members as well as Conservative members of this house are anxious to have bilingualism established throughout Canada. As the minister has said, he is in favour of

bilingualism and so are we. We may not be able to speak as loudly or with the eloquence of the hon. member, but even though we do not get up very often in the house to talk about bilingualism the hon. member might be surprised to know of the gatherings we have in connection with bilingualism and justice to be rendered to French Canadians at large. I do not want to be too hard on him or on his party, but if we-
Be as hard as you wish; I am prepared for you.

So am I for you. I have seen others in 25 years. Just to give a little history, I remember that in 1934 a motion was presented by Mr. Boulanger, the then member for Bellechasse, but it was talked out. Then there was a motion by Mr. Gobeil which was talked out as well. In 1936 Bill No. 82 was presented by Mr. Dunning, then minister of finance, and under section 15 as I remember it there was a long and fiery discussion on the whole subject of bilingual money.
Mr. Bennett, then leader of the opposition and chief of the Conservative party, stated in the debate that it was wrong of the Liberal party to bring up that question on the floor of the house. He said there was bilingual money because he had ordered the printing of French and English bills. It was not French and English on the same bill; there were French bills and English bills, and he considered that that was bilingualism.
If my hon. friend wants to read some good speeches on this question I would refer him to one made by his former leader, Mr. Bennett, who said that bilingualism in Canada was a concession to French Canadians. The Right Hon. Mr. Lapointe said we did not need concessions, that it was our right to speak both languages, to speak French in the house, to have bilingual money and bilingual cheques. Let him read the speech made by the Right Hon. Minister of Agriculture and he will have something to talk about. Let him read the speech by Mr. Cardin and he will see what bilingualism means to the Liberal party. He will see that the Liberal party has done its best to spread bilingualism in Canada.
As the minister has said, there is no technical difficulty, but there are other difficulties. My hon. friend, who is a good French-speaking Acadian, knows of those difficulties as well as I do.
What are they?
The people in your district know what are the causes for these delays in bilingualism in Canada. You know that.
That is not an answer to my question.
Just go through your district and you will find the answer in your soul or heart.
He has not one.

Yes, he has one. We know the difficulties, and so does the hon. member. Not very long ago an hon. member of his own party asked the Minister of Finance why he had sent out formulas printed in French to the province of Ontario.
Forget about it.

I will not forget about it. If I had been aware that this debate would take place I would be able to give my hon. friend the reference.
(Translation) :

We, in the province of Quebec, receive English forms and are not always complaining.
(Text):

We have given a good example which has been followed in Canada. Canada is considered to be the prototype of bilingualism and we should be proud of that. Let me give a personal illustration. I have four children who all speak two languages, some of them speaking three and four. My wife is one of the best French-Canadian women to be found among French-Canadian women and she taught English to her husband and her four children. That is a good sign that French Canadians are in favour of bilingualism. They give a good example in that way. Lots of Englishspeaking Canadians follow that example. If that practice were universal there would be no difficulties left in Canada. We have had an example tonight where the Englishspeaking Minister of Finance answered my hon. friend in good French. If examples like that are followed we will soon see bilingualism flourishing throughout Canada.
My hon. friend said we were going into an election, and that we have many declarations to make. Yes, we are. We are going to dig into the past and present records. That is our right and privilege, and we are going to do it. We are preparing for it as my hon. friend is preparing. I do not want to let my temper get the best of me. I want to sit down. But may I tell my hon. friend to continue to set a good example, to continue to emphasize the fact that we are a bilingual country and to continue to try to get this belief shared by all his fellow members of the Conservative party.
Supply-Finance
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I wish to say to to the hon. member for Portneuf (Mr. Gauthier) that it is not a question of French Canadians setting an example and it is especially not a question of the French Canadians of the province of Quebec asking for privileges. We do not care-
Others have said so before you.
It is not the hon. member for Portneuf who said it before me, nor will he say it after me.
Of course not; it was said by the Hon. Mr. Lapointe, a Liberal.
The hon. member for Portneuf seems to believe that French Canadians should be satisfied with what they are getting.
I never said that.
I did not interrupt the hon. member for Portneuf when he was speaking and I would ask him to let me finish my remarks.
You don't speak loudly enough.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order!

I am surprised to see how subservient the hon. member for Portneuf and his Liberal colleagues are when their party is in power, when they were so vocal in favour of bilingual money and postage stamps for the whole of Canada when they were sitting on the opposition side in 1930. It is the responsibility of this government to grant bilingual cheques to Canadians, whether they live in the province of Quebec, in British Columbia, in Alberta, or in the constituency of my hon. friend, the county of Gloucester. This is a right that we are claiming, a right granted to us under the constitution of this country and of which nobody can deprive us. We are only asking the present government to recognize this right and, along with the hon. member for Portneuf and his fellow members from the Liberal party, I admit that that party has given us the most, so far as bilingualism in Canada is concerned. I ask the government tonight, to give us bilingual cheques, because I know that in the past it has been fair to us and that it could do us justice once more.
That is all I want to say tonight to the Minister of Finance. I am astonished to note that the hon. member for Portneuf seems to believe that we are indulging in opposition merely for the sake of it. We are just asking-

Supply-Finance
Mr. Chairman, on a question of privilege-
There is no question of privilege.
Yes, there is. The hon. member is distorting the meaning of what I have just said.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Chicoutimi must resume his seat when an hon. member raises a question of privilege. The hon. member for Portneuf has risen on a question of privilege and in order to know whether he is entitled to rise for that purpose, I must at least listen to what he has to say.

Mr. Chairman, the rules forbid an hon. member to impute motives to one of his colleagues. The hon. member for Chicoutimi, in distorting my words, has said all sorts of things which are but figments of his mind. I would simply ask him to understand, once and for all, that we are in favour of bilingualism, 150 per cent if need be. Is that sufficiently clear?
Give us bilingual cheques.
Mr. Chairman, in reply to the hon. member for Portneuf, I must tell him that I did not impute anything to him. I cannot impute to him any ideas, because he has none.

Is it you who has
none, or I?
I am speaking of the member for Portneuf. You cannot impute intelligence to anybody if he is without it or has to borrow it from someone else. You cannot impute motives to somebody who shows none.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not believe the hon.
member for Chicoutimi is allowed to say of another member that he has to borrow intelligence. I believe he should withdraw those words.

If the hon. member for Portneuf or anybody else in this house has been hurt by what I have said, I am ready to withdraw.
Once more, we are asking for bilingual cheques, just as the Liberals asked the Bennett government for bilingual banknotes.
(Text):

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Administration of various acts and costs of special functions-
112.	Construction or acquisition of new equipment, $740,953.

I should like to ask the minister what is the total estimated cost of the additions and alterations to the mint. I

should also like to ask him as to what extent the estimated construction and acquisition of this new equipment will facilitate the production at the mint.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The total acquisition of equipment for this year is $740,953. That represents the major part of the new equipment to be put in the expanded facilities at the mint.
Coinage has increased from 5,027,507 pieces in 1908 to well over 100 million pieces at the present time. My understanding is that this increase in the physical facilities of the mint is the first major increase that has taken place since 1908.
The mint has been operating at more than rated capacity, if I may use the industrial phrase. The demand for subsidiary coin, due no doubt to the large increase in the volume of business transactions, has been extremely great. The master of the mint is hopeful that this equipment will be installed before the end of the current fiscal year.
I must say that I should like to take this opportunity to pay a tribute to the efficient work which is being done at the mint. For instance, in addition to the large volume of regular work which has been going on, the mint has been able to get a design approved and turn out over 3 million medallions which are now ready to be distributed to school children throughout Canada, through the provinces, to commemorate Her Majesty's coronation.
I do not know whether or not I gave my hon. friend the particular information he asked for, but that gives him an indication of the increase in the volume of business turned out by the mint since the original facilities were installed.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
113.	Administration of employees' instalment purchase plan, including sale and delivery of Canada savings bonds to government employees; and of employees' group insurance plans, $97,310.

Will the
minister explain why this is a separate item, and in particular will he say why it comes quite separate from an item on page 18 entitled "cost of issuing new loans"? That item is about half-way down the page.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. This item provides for the administrative expenses of the employees' instalment purchase plan which permits employees of the public service of Canada and naval, army and air force personnel to purchase Canada savings bonds by means of payroll deductions. The employee arranges for the financing for a period of one year and subsequently acquires his bond. Provision is also included for the administration of the public service hospital-medical plan to which

about 58,330 federal civil servants have subscribed. I suppose it is fair to say that it is analogous to a section in a large industrial organization which would provide for the payroll subscriptions to Canada savings bonds and perhaps to the various charitable campaigns where payroll deductions are authorized.
How many would be involved? The amount is nearly $100,000. Offhand, that would seem to be a good deal of money. How many would be involved in the service?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The total staff are 35, I am informed, 29 on the employees' instalment purchase plan and six on the medical insurance plan. There is a decrease of some staff this year.
Continuing at the bottom of page 17, the first statutory item, the increase is $19 million. Is that wholly due to rising interest rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Principally. The increase is in the interest on the funded debt which amounts to $19 million, as my hon. friend has pointed out, and on the unfunded debt the increase is about $13-3 million. The increase is due to two factors, first the increase in the interest rate, and also the increased payments on the principal amount of the superannuation fund. My hon. friend will recall that I pointed out that interest is now being paid on the full actuarial liability of the fund, and that represents an increase over the preceding year. It would be on the unfunded debt, of course.
The funded debt was also increased by $122 million, was it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Gross; that is correct.
I wonder if the minister could say anything about future policy with respect to bond issues. A few months ago a bond issue for $100 million was made at 3-75 per cent interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: 3-76 per cent.

At the time it was issued it was stated in the newspapers it would be government policy to refund other issues at a similar rate of interest. If that should be the policy, then debt charges would steadily increase. Although the minister has taken a good deal of credit from the fact that over a period of years we have reduced the net debt, nevertheless debt charges would be steadily climbing. After all, the people of Canada will be more interested in debt charges than in the figure of the national debt. It does not help the people very much to reduce the national debt if debt charges are going to keep climbing.
Supply-Finance

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think I said it was the government's intention to refund further maturing obligations at the same rate or a similar rate of interest.
No, it was in the newspapers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The statement did not come from me. During the current fiscal year we have no long-term bonds maturing, so it will not be necessary to enter the market to refund any long-term obligations. We have the usual treasury bills and some short-term obligations which will fall due and those will be refunded, presumably, at the going market rate.
As my hon. friend knows, interest rates both here and in the United States have risen somewhat. That rise in interest rates is, of course, reflected both in the prices of longterm bonds which are outstanding and in the interest which has to be paid when maturing obligations are refunded.

On page 18 under the heading: "Commission for payment of interest on public debt, services of fiscal agents, London, registrar's fees, etc." the amount is more than doubled. It is increased from $326,100 to $704,600. Why is that?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The entire increase in this item is in respect of the commission for payment of coupon and fully registered interest to the chartered banks in Canada as a result of a change in the remuneration. Whereas the previous commission was based on J of 1 per cent of the total face value of coupons, subsequent to April 1, 1952, commission at the above rate could in no case be less than 2J cents per coupon.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Payments to municipalities-
Grants to municipalities in lieu of taxes on federal property-
114.	To provide for payments to municipalities in accordance with the Municipal Grants Act. and the rural municipal grants regulations established by order in council of August 6. 1952, P.C. 3729: and to provide for payments to municipalities under order in council of July 19, 1950, P.C. 3456, in respect of the cost of medical and hospital services and supplies furnished to federal employees and other persons specified therein, $2,701,300.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to comment on this item at some little length because it seems to me this is a case where the municipalities that are already having a very bad time are just being shoved down a little bit further in the mud. I wish to bring to the attention of the committee certain rather important considerations, though I repeat that I realize that if everything I asked were to be done it would only be a step on the way to solving the problem.

Supply-Finance
The minister will realize that I hesitate to argue for additional expenditure, but it seems to me there are times when justice is involved and should be done. Indeed, the minister seems to have put himself a little bit in the position of the priest and the Levite who, when the gentleman fell among thieves, passed by on the other side. I hope my words may turn the minister into a good Samaritan, because that is what we need here.
Now, Mr. Chairman, the minister has recommended $2,701,300 for this purpose, but let us recall to our minds briefly the background of this act.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but I merely want to have an understanding. On the first item, administration, we had a general discussion and it seems to me that the speech which the hon. member is initiating is one that could have been made on the first item. We are studying the details of this vote at page 190, and the discussion must be strictly relevant according to our standing order. I know that his remarks will be relevant to the act under which this money is being voted and agreed to by parliament, and I do not want to curtail the discussion. The understanding, however, is that the general discussion is supposed to embrace all activities of the department. This subject could perhaps have been more appropriately dealt with at that time.

Mr. Chairman, as always I defer to you; but I must confess that it does come to me as a great surprise that you are questioning my right to discuss this item. I believe that every word I shall say will be strictly relevant. I propose to argue that this item should be larger, and I cannot do so without giving you my reasons. I shall make my comments as brief as I can, but I confess I shall probably take ten minutes or thereabouts to outline what I have to say. I submit with deference that surely this is a proper place to argue about this item, about the attitude of the minister under this act, and about what is supposed to be done under it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member should not be surprised, because this is a rule that has been followed very closely. In the discussion of estimates of certain departments which we have studied from time to time this session there may have been departures from that ruling. That does not mean that a departure in respect of one department- and I have in mind the Department of National Health and Welfare-should be made the occasion for a departure from the rule

for another department. I am making the point now in an attempt to have the rule observed at the commencement.
What I wish to point out is that the minister apparently takes the attitude that this is really an act of grace. He takes the attitude, as expressed in the act-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The minister does not do that; the British North America Act does.

The minister takes the attitude that the B.N.A. Act is sacrosanct. My answer to that is that we have a situation today in which the whole fabric of our economy has changed. I am not going to dwell on that. But I do want to point out that the minister goes on then to say that it is fair to deal only with those cases where there is more than an average amount of federal property, because he says that in giving effect to a federal program of this sort we should recognize that the presence of federal property within a municipality normally brings certain definite benefits to the municipality. No doubt that is true, but it is equally true of other business in the municipality. I suggest that that argument really has not value whatever.
I wish to point out what has happened to the municipalities, and the distress into which they have been sinking. I shall seek to show that the minister's proposal has been chiselled and cut down in various ways, so that it is reduced to its very lowest terms. The municipalities have not been treated generously or fairly under the terms of the act itself. I wish to give a few figures for the record, just to show what has happened in the municipalities in the last few years since the war. At this point I am quoting from a speech delivered by the mayor of Ottawa on October 22, 1952. She points out that in the period from 1930 to 1948 dominion taxation increased 718 per cent, provincial taxation 303 per cent and municipal taxation 50 per cent. In 1930 the dominion absorbed 38-6 per cent of the tax revenues in Canada, and in 1948 took 67-5 per cent; in 1930 the provinces took 22 per cent and in 1948 they took 19-8 per cent but the municipalities, which in 1930 enjoyed 39-4 per cent, had but 12-7 per cent in 1948.
To express in a word what this burden means to the municipalities a friend of mine, who is very familiar with municipal affairs, says that the public is aware of constantly increasing assessments on their homes and shops; of constantly increasing mill rates and of constantly increasing municipal taxes. There is an awareness of poor local roads

and streets caused by the high cost of construction and repair, of the high cost of fire services and education. Each time a new school is built, the tremendous increase in costs is published in local newspapers and constantly agitated before local boards of education and councils.
To show the plight to which municipalities are reduced, I cannot do better than quote from a statement by Dr. Althouse, which appeared in the Globe and Mail of April 7, 1953. Dr. Althouse, the chief director of education for Ontario, expressed himself as follows:
Education authorities are expecting a three-year financial crisis and unless the additions to schools are kept down to the essential this difficult period may be extended .	.	. Dr. Althouse warned
that all school boards must co-operate otherwise teachers' salaries would be endangered.
Now I want to say a word as to the effect of this on housing. When we translate this into terms of ordinary day to day life, we put a heavy burden on home owners and particularly on our young married people who are seeking to establish homes. We all have the deepest sympathy with this problem. We all recognize that one of the greatest obstacles in the way of establishing a home is the high taxes.
Upon inquiry I find that municipal taxes on real estate in 1952 amounted to some $500 million. On the basis of the government owning between 4 and 5 per cent, if they paid full rates their taxes would be from $20 to $25 million instead of $2-7 million. At this point I again quote the mayor of Ottawa to show the way in which this legislation is chiselled and haggled in order to keep the municipalities down to the very lowest terms. She has this to say:
There is no logical ground lor taking the average concentration of dominion government property across Canada, finding it to be 4 per cent: then fixing that as the arbitrary figure and maintaining that payment for municipal services, given to the dominion, will be made only in municipalities where the government property exceeds this 4 per cent of total assessments plus government holdings.
She points out also that by arranging to plant new government properties in municipalities with less than 4 per cent, the government can reduce their obligations still lower. Then she goes on to say:
A second inequity is that, while every citizen must accept the municipality's own assessed values as a basis of tax levy, with the right of appeal open, the dominion authority, through its own officials, rejects the municipal assessment valuations and put its own "accepted value" on the properties in the judgment of its own officials and with no right of appeal whatever.
Further she sets out five more inequities.
Third, the dominion, on its own decision, again with no right of appeal left open to the munic-
Supply-Finance
ipality, excludes from taxation items assessable, if privately owned . . .
There is a long list of items given, but I cannot take time to read them.
Fourth, the way in which the dominion authority then calculates the tax levy, having made its own valuations, and taken off 4 per cent to start with, tends to be arbitrary and inequitable, . . .
Fifth, after these various contractions have been applied there is another purely arbitrary mathematical "squeeze"-only 75 per cent of the amount then calculated as due to the municipality as the grant in lieu of taxes is taken.
Sixth, when the grant has been finally calculated, a system of deductions comes in, whereby the dominion officials deduct what they calculate as their valuations of all services which they themselves provide for themselves.
Seventh, a series of withdrawals then enters, whereby the dominion officials withdraw, on their own calculations again, the value of services they deem to have been rendered by dominion services to the city.
I have tried to indicate, first of all, the arbitrary way in which the whole matter is approached. Second, I have tried to indicate the cheese-paring manner in which it is done. We are told it is solely a matter of grace which is to be subject to discretionary determination. Then we are told that the presence of government property brings certain definite benefits to the municipality, and for that reason 4 per cent is justified.
My submission to the minister, Mr. Chairman, is that when we look at the position of the municipalities, we find as I briefly indicated that the federal government revenues have multiplied many times, the provincial revenues several times, and the municipalities have only increased their revenue by half.
Meanwhile their burdens have vastly increased. As we all know, at one time the whole of real estate was able to carry a very large part of the load, but now it is only one of the many forms of raising revenue. The most lucrative forms have been taken over, as we all know, by the dominion.
Furthermore the government has refused one other method of assistance which the municipalities had suggested, through the remission of sales tax, so we are left with the situation that the municipalities are in a worse position with very little prospect of any improvement. There has been no suggestion of improvement from the government that I am aware of; the government holds out no tolerable prospect of relief to them. Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is not a situation which either common sense or a sense of justice should tolerate. The position of the municipalities has gone from bad to worse. I have read a whole list of what I call chiselling, which is indulged in. I realize that it is partly due to the legislation, though not all. It is partly due to a series of regulations.

speechtext:
Before we pass beyond this item I should like to say a few words. I have listened to the discussion in regard to the adequacy or inadequacy of the provision that is made in this case, and I must say that there is something very anomalous in hearing the minister refer to the British North America Act as the explanation for the position of the government in this instance. It is interesting to hear the government express its faith in the British North America Act when it affords a convenient defence for an improper way of dealing with the municipalities in regard to their plight at this time.
To examine the adequacy of this item it is necessary to look at the over-all picture. If you examine the over-all picture you will find there are a number of considerations which the minister has not dealt with, and which seem to call for consideration of the situation with which the municipalities are confronted at this time. There is no use pretending that we are going to get down to a detailed examination of every component figure that enters into these items. Sometimes there may be an impression outside of parliament that in the discussion of these items it is possible to go into a general bookkeeping examination. That is not so. The most that is possible is to deal with certain principles.
Already this session hope had been expressed that the government would recognize the position of the municipalities. A motion was placed before the house dealing with the sales tax and the excise tax. That has been disposed of, and I do not propose to raise in connection with this item the discussion that took place at that time. The fact, however, is that from one end of Canada to the other mayors and reeves are expressing their grave concern about the position of the municipalities and their ability to carry out the mounting burden that is imposed upon them.
I do not propose to exchange arguments with the minister about which party has shown more consideration in cases of this kind. The fact is that we are confronted with an entirely new situation. Never before, either in war or in peace, under any other government was an amount taken from the people in taxes such as is being taken in this present year. It is today the highest exaction there has ever been. The hon. member for Greenwood showed the progressive and increasing percentage of the tax dollar taken by the dominion up to 1948, but we can carry it beyond that. It is going progressively higher all the time. Last year 78 "cents out of every tax dollar came to the government of Canada, leaving only 22 cents

available to both the municipalities and the provincial governments.
To attempt to place this picture before the house in terms of what was before the fathers of confederation in 1867 is to deal with this in terms of utter unreality. There is no need to suggest any departure from the basic principles of the British North America Act, to suggest that there is a problem that has to be dealt with here that was never contemplated at that time, and never could have been contemplated.
Let us just take one aspect alone of the problems of the municipalities. Certainly in 1867 no one ever heard of civil defence, in the manner in which we now understand those words. No one ever heard of civil defence in the way those words are now understood after the two world wars. Now we have these tremendous demands made upon municipalities to do their share in a very special form of defence which never before was regarded as an obligation of the municipalities. Yet we have the extraordinary situation that those municipalities, which are called upon to buy fire equipment and defence equipment of various kinds, must pay sales tax and excise tax to the Canadian government on that very equipment they must buy as part of the general defence of Canada.
Under those circumstances it is unrealistic to suggest that the needs of municipalities are being met by some inadequate formula such as that which we now have before us. With these other demands, and with the unjust burden of sales tax and excise tax not only on their ordinary requirements for roads, schools and other things of that nature, but also for civil defence, which is really part of the general defence of Canada, most certainly the government of Canada should deal with this subject in a way which recognizes their needs.
As I said before, it is not within the power of members of parliament to deal in exact and minute detail with each of these problems. We are dealing with the Department of Finance, the department which has the over-all responsibility for finance. What is before us now is mainly the general set of principles which guide the responsibilities and administration of that department.
I submit that the municipalities of this country need a new deal at this time. The municipalities of Canada, where the very bedrock of our democracy rests, require greater consideration. Their burdens have increased; their responsibilities have expanded, just as have the responsibilities of the government of Canada. They have

51G7
within the municipalities, and under their school boards, the direct responsibility for education, along with the provincial governments.
I do submit that even at this stage of the session the Minister of Finance would be well advised to let this item stand, and inform the house that he is prepared to reconsider it and bring before the house some provision which, at least in regard to assessment on property occupied by the dominion government, will extend some measure of justice to the municipalities which are carrying such heavy burdens.
At the time these exemptions were originally provided by the British North America Act, the only type of property that was contemplated was that property which would be required for services of a very limited nature, such as direct government services. There were none of these great corporate emanations of government such as we have today. This could go on to the point where, in many municipalities, a very large part of the taxable property would be under the control of the government of Canada, and where municipalities would be called upon to rely upon the discretion of the federal government as to what they were prepared to do.
I rise at this time to ask the Minister of Finance, even at this stage in the discussion of his estimates, and at this stage of the session, to reconsider the position of the government in regard to the position of the municipalities in the matter of taxation.

I should like to comment briefly on this item, and I am quite sure the minister is quite familiar with the matters that have been raised in connection with it. This matter is of such importance that one could speak much longer than a moment or two, but I realize the lateness of the hour and I appreciate that the minister wants to complete his estimates tonight.
When this item was first included in the estimates the Prime Minister stated that it was a provisional scheme and suggested that it be tried for a year, after which changes could be made if it proved to be unsatisfactory. As the minister well knows from the representations which have been made, from the east at any rate, the situation has not proved satisfactory to Nova Scotia. In the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne last fall the hon. member for Halifax placed figures on the record in connection with this, which I do not intend to repeat except to give one or two of the highlights.
As you know, this is on a per capita basis, 50 cents per head for every person of population as found by the bureau of statistics, which amount is divided between the student registration. The result is that last year the universities of Nova Scotia received $92.45 per student; those of Ontario received $126.28; Saskatchewan received $180.73 and Newfoundland, $483.16. I do not wish to repeat and put on the record statements made before the Massey commission and by the Prime Minister that this is recognized as a national problem, that the universities are making a national contribution. I simply say that if the universities are making a national contribution, they should be treated on a national basis.
The universities of Nova Scotia are the only ones in Canada which receive no assistance from the provincial government. The universities in every other province receive such assistance. To a minor extent there are grants in Nova Scotia for teachers amounting to $5,000 in the case of Acadia; $5,000 in the case of St. Francis Xavier, and certain grants

to Dalhousie for professional teaching. Other than that they receive no grants from the provincial treasury and are receiving this small payment per student.
I know the minister has given consideration to this matter. I know he has received briefs from the various universities. In the case of veterans the grant was on the basis of so much per student. If that was considered a fair way to approach that problem, I think consideration should be given to these grants. At any rate there should be a national average, and each university should be paid on that basis. If it means additional payments, well and good; but the system is not equitable and fair as it operates at the moment.
I quite realize that having come so far with his estimates the minister will not make any change. I do not want to write a letter, although the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre did, but if he wants to create for himself a niche in the hall of immortality he will place an additional supplementary estimate before us to level this up and provide a better basis of payment, because this one is most inequitable.

subtopic: PAYMENTS MADE TO MUNICIPALITIES BY THE MUNICIPAL GRANTS BUREAU OF THE DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I want to support the hon. member for Annapolis-Kings, and I am not going to be very long in doing it. Despite what the senior member for Halifax had to say, this is a pretty live issue in Nova Scotia, and has been for the past year. I could make a long speech on the matter, but I shall just read an editorial which appeared in the Sydney Post-Record, of Friday, July 5, 1952 which sets it all out in a very clear manner. It reads:
Federal grants in aid to Canadian universities have been allocated in a way to put Nova Scotia at a serious disadvantage in comparison with the other provinces. Surely this was not the intention of the Massey report recommendations which the government undertook to implement.
In the distribution of the grants for 1951-52, Nova Scotia received the smallest amount per student of any province in the dominion. This injustice must not be repeated for 1952-53. Parliament voted $7,100,000 for assistance to Canadian universities. The total amount was distributed at the rate of 50 cents a head, according to provincial population, but without regard to the number of eligible students in each province.
Mainly because the professional schools of Nova Scotia serve the four Atlantic provinces, Nova Scotia has a high proportion of eligible students under the scheme. The result was that, in the 1951-52 distribution, Nova Scotia's allotment was only $92.45 per student, compared with $126.28 in Ontario, $180.73 in Saskatchewan and $483.16 in Newfoundland. In effect, Nova Scotia is penalized for having a high proportion of eligible students.
Prime Minister St. Laurent has agreed with the findings of the Massey commission that the universities perform a national service. Since the grants are made admittedly as a national assistance, it would seem logical that they should be allocated at a national rate, as was done with the D.V.A. grants.
It is definitely unfair that a student in Nova Scotia should benefit less, through aid to his university, than a student in another province. In the

Supply-Finance
light of the facts Ottawa should re-examine the matter and work out a more equitable means of distribution. It's not to be believed that the government deliberately wishes to penalize Nova Scotia.
I think that summarizes the case clearly, and I would suggest that the minister and his advisers take another look at the matter when a reallocation is made.

Mr. Chairman, there is a matter which I should like to raise under this heading, in connection with small loans. It has been of interest to the department, I know; yet the department finds itself powerless to act in a situation which has within it all the elements of a racket. There is in Toronto an outfit known as Consolidated Finance Corporation, and they have been sending out to potential victims this sheet of paper which I have in my hand and which states:
Here's the answer to your debt worries . . .
They manage to answer the debt worries, so they believe, without coming within the purview of the department, which I must say is doing an extraordinarily good job of work in the small loans field. This is what the corporation states, and I think the committee ought to know what is happening so that the corporation can be exposed. The pamphlet states:
The present high cost of living makes it often very difficult to meet the demands of all your creditors.
The result: You get phone calls and letters of demand from your creditors, garnishees on your pay, court judgments and seizures, lawyers' actions . . . problems upon problems!
Now, with one visit to the office of Consolidated Finance you can shed your problems. Simply make a list of all debts you owe for: hospitals, automobile, furniture, jewelry, groceries, doctors, lawyers, loan companies, etc.-Then see us.
What happens is this. The victim goes to the Consolidated Finance Corporation. He owes, let us say, some $200 to several creditors. Consolidated Finance says to the victim, "We are prepared to tackle this for you. Of course, this is not a small loan business, but what we shall do is this. You add up all the accounts you owe, and then pay us 25 per cent as an overriding fee, and we shall go to the various companies concerned and state that you are paying so much money a month to each of them. You will give us the money and we will disburse it. But first of all, of course, this overriding fee of 25 per cent has to be paid." Consolidated Finance gets that fee. It is part of the racket which we too often find in the small loans

business. I know the department is doing its best to clean it up. I should also like to know whether there is any way whereby we can stop firms such as Consolidated Finance Corporation from acting in such a way with innocent people who find themselves in debt, who need help and who invariably go to the wrong people for it.
